One of the clearest pressures on private renters is the growing concentration of holiday lets and second homes in some areas. In my town, a noticeable share of homes has shifted away from long‑term rentals, pushing up rents and reducing the sense of community. Local licensing or caps on holiday lets, with clear rules about primary residence and straightforward enforcement, could protect long‑term stock without unfairly burdening legitimate operators. Any licensing income should fund more inspections and targeted support to help landlords bring properties up to standard. 

Alongside this, we need stronger baseline standards for all private rentals: mandatory safety checks, carbon monoxide alarms, and clearly enforceable energy efficiency improvements. Create straightforward routes for landlords to upgrade, such as grants or low‑interest loans, with a phased, proportionate rollout so small landlords aren’t overwhelmed. Promote longer tenancies by default where possible, and ensure deposits are protected with quick, fair dispute resolution.

These changes should come with practical support for councils to enforce rules and a light touch on compliant landlords. Pairing them with covenanted, affordable homes in Build‑to‑Rent schemes can help maintain supply, while improving security and standards for private renters.

From what I’ve seen and heard among my peers in England, it’s possible to improve security for private renters while keeping a healthy rental market. I back stronger grounds, longer notice periods for no-fault evictions, and clear appeal rights. If a landlord wants to end a tenancy without fault, six months’ notice, with a narrow, transparent set of legitimate reasons and a straightforward route to appeal, would give tenants real stability and time to plan. Retaliation protections are essential too—if you raise a repair issue or complain about conditions, eviction shouldn’t be a punishment. 

On affordability, I support rent caps or stabilization alongside targeted subsidies. annual increases tied to the lower of CPI or local wage growth (with sensible exceptions for genuine capital improvements) would stop sudden spikes, while subsidies help those on lower incomes stay in good homes. These measures must be designed to avoid squeezing supply, so they should sit with the Build-to-Rent approach we already back, including affordability covenants and professional management.

I’ve seen friends struggle with no-fault evictions and rising rents; stronger protections would have reduced insecurity and disruption, especially for students and graduates. Paired with ongoing investment in good-quality, well-managed rental stock, these changes can deliver fairer, more sustainable rents without dampening investment in new homes.

As an organisation with experience across rural and urban England, we support a balanced package of changes to improve security, affordability and standards for private renters wihteout undermining a sustainable rental market. First, introduce tenure‑stability measures: rent caps or indexation linked to local affordability (for example CPI plus a modest margin) with regional variation and targeted subsidies for lower‑income households to constrain excessiveee increases while protecting supply. Caps should apply to existing tenancies but allow sensible increases for new-builds and genuine improvements, to encourage investment where it is most needed. Second, deliver fast low‑cost dispute resolution: expand funded tenant advicr services, broaden mediation, and streamline tribunals so issuee around deposits, repairs and notices are resolved quickly and tenants feel safe voicing concerns. Third, enforceable safety, habitability and energy efficiency standards: set robust minimum standards with funded retrofit support for landlords, helping to raise EPC ratings and reduce bills for tenants. In rural areas, provide targeted incentives to improve older stock. Together, these measures protect tenants, support stability, and preserve a viable private rental sector that can respond to housing demand.

From my experience as a renter in England, the best way to improve security, affordability and standards is to push more affordable supply while keeping a sustainable rental market. That means reforming planning to unlock brownfield sites and support build-to-rent with long-term, transparent tenancies and predictable rents. It should also include incentives to convert underused offices and shops into genuinely affordable private rental homes, funded through low-interest loans or tax relief, rather than pushing people further into overcrowded or distant locations.

Expanding social housing supply remains essential to ease pressure on private rents. And we must reset landlord responsibility with enforceable safety, habitability and energy standards. Require regular gas and electrical safety checks, smoke and CO alarms, damp management, and accessible design where needed. Make energy efficiency a default: minimum EPC rating C for new and renewed tenancies, with funded retrofit support to upgrade insulation, heating and draught-proofing so bills are lower and health improves.

Local examples matter: in our town there are derelict mills and empty shops that could become affordable flats; a damp flat I know was fixed only after a retrofit program. Clear delivery pipelines, strong enforcement and support for landlords to upgrade will keep the market sustainable while protecting tenants.

Support stronger controls on holiday lets and second homes through local licensing to protect long-term rentals, while boosting affordable supply via planning reform, build-to-rent incentives, brownfield and social housing. Also promote multi-year tenancies and easier renewals to stabilise households and communities.

i really think in our communities across Wales, private renters often face insecurity and unpredictable costs, even though the private rented sector remains essential to prevent gaps in supply. To improve security, affordability and standards without harming the sustainability of the market, I’d support a balanced package built on longer tenancies, clearer renewal processes, strong safety and energy standards, and funded retrofit support. This would help stability at home while protecting health, comfort, and bills, and it would keep landlords and tenants working together rather than at odds.

What I’d like to see:

- Longer, clearer tenancies with easy renewals. A default minimum term of two years, with automatic renewal unless a landlord has a clear, justified ground to end the tenancy. Tenants would have predictable renewals and a right to stay on improving terms if the property is well maintained. At renewal, any rent increase should be transparent and reasonable, with a cap or formula tied to inflation and energy costs rather than open-ended hikes. This would reduce churn, limit moving costs, and strengthen community ties, which are especially important in our smaller Welsh towns and coastal communities.

- Clear safety, habitability and energy standards with retrofit support. Properties should meet minimum safety requirements (gas safety checks, electrical safety where applicable, smoke and CO detectors, damp-and-mould prevention measures) and a baseline energy efficiency standard. Given rising bills and poor indoor conditions in some homes, there must be funded retrofit support to lift energy performance and comfort. An accessible Welsh retrofit fund could cover insulation, draught-proofing, and energy-system upgrades (for example, efficient boilers or heat pumps) with reasonable landlord contributions and streamlined processes for tenants to access these improvements.

- Fair, enforceable standards with strong enforcement. Local authorities should have clear powers to investigate complaints, enforce repairs, and take action against persistent non-compliance. Transparent reporting of safety failures and energy improvements would help tenants choose well and drive landlords to maintain their properties.

- Incentives to upskill and invest in the private sector. Retrofit and safety upgrades should come with incentives for landlords—grants, low-interest loans, or tax relief—so that meeting higher standards does not push rents beyond affordability or reduce the supply of rental homes. Supporting small-scale landlords with guidance and access to local tradespeople would also sustain local jobs and keep work within communities.

- Provisions that protect supply during transition. While raising standards and extending tenancies, we must guard against unintended reductions in rental supply. Sunset clauses for temporary controls, phased rollouts, and ongoing evaluation would help policymakers adjust rules if they risk reducing the number of available homes.

- Examples from our experience. In some Welsh towns, families have faced damp housing and unaffordable energy bills due to poor insulation and leaky homes. A two-year tenancy with a commitment to upgrade where needed would reduce displacement, while retrofit funding would cut bills for households already living on tight incomes. When properties are well maintained and efficient, neighbours stay longer, and families build stronger local networks and skills through local trades.

Overall, I believe a combination of longer tenancies, clear renewal rights, robust safety and energy standards, and targeted retrofit funding can deliver steadier homes, lower bills, and healthier living environments, while keeping a sustainable private rented market that supports and strengthens communities across Wales.

Thank you for giving us the chance to contribute. From our broader work on delivering good quality homes and protecting communities, I think the private rented sector can be made safer, more affordable and more reliable without undermining a sustainable market. The key is a clear, well funded package of safety, energy efficiency and tenancy security that works for tenants, landlords and local authorities alike.

- Enforceable safety, habitability and energy standards with retrofit support
- Make safety and habitable living conditions non-negotiable: landlords should meet comprehensive safety standards as a baseline. This includes mandatory annual gas safety checks, electrical safety inspections every five years, and legally required functioning smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in all privately rented homes. Damp, mould and ventilation issues must be addressed promptly with clear timetables for remediation. These basics directly protect health and reduce emergency cost burdens on families.
- Raise energy efficiency standards in line with broader climate goals. Aim for a minimum standard of EPC C for private rentals, with a pathway to EPC B where feasible, and a clear obligation on landlords to make cost-effective energy improvements. To ease the burden, provide funded retrofit support—grants, low-interest loans or tied-in schemes through local authorities or partnerships with housing associations—so small landlords can upgrade without risking viability. This would reduce energy bills for tenants, improve comfort, and reduce disputes about inefficient heating.
- Ensure robust delivery and enforcement: local councils should have stronger powers to levy penalties where standards aren’t met, and there should be mandatory reporting on safety compliance and energy improvements. A simple, transparent reporting framework helps tenants know their rights and helps councils target pockets of poor quality housing.
- Tenancy security and stability
- Promote longer, more secure tenancies by default. Moving to minimum terms of, say, two years with straightforward renewal options would give families stability, reduce churn and the costs and upheaval associated with moving, and help sustain communities. Clear and predictable renewal processes also help landlords plan and invest in their properties with more confidence.
- Balance tenancy certainty with legitimate landlord rights. Landlords should still be able to end tenancies for genuine reasons (non-payment, anti-social behaviour, property sale, etc.), but the default should be longer leases and easier renewal. A predictable framework reduces disputes and gives tenants the confidence to invest in the home and community.
- Rent setting and affordability protections: allow rents to reflect genuine costs but implement safeguards to prevent sudden or excessive increases between renewals. Tenants should have a clear, fair process for increases, with notice periods and a cap tied to reasonable indexes or costs, so households can budget with some certainty.
- Support and dispute resolution: improve access to practical support for both tenants and landlords. Clear guidance on rights and responsibilities, a straightforward route to redress, and faster resolution of problems will reduce disputes and improve trust in the sector.
- Practical examples from our area
- In our town, a privately rented property with longstanding damp and high bills benefited from a targeted retrofit funded through a local retrofit scheme. Cavity insulation and a more efficient boiler cut energy use and bills materially, and the tenant was able to stay in the home rather than move. With a two-year tenancy in place and a straightforward renewal process, the tenant felt more secure in their neighbourhood and engaged with local services and schools, which strengthened community links.
- Another case involved a small landlord who faced the administrative burden of compliance. A government-backed retrofit loan and access to guidance reduced the perceived risks, enabled essential improvements and allowed a longer tenancy to be offered at a fair rent. This shows what can be achieved when policy design recognises the realities of private landlords while prioritising tenant health and affordability.

In short, changes that combine enforceable safety and energy efficiency standards with funded retrofit support, plus longer, clearer tenancy relationships and fair cost protections, will improve security for private renters, reduce energy bills, and sustain a healthy rental market. It aligns with our broader aim of making best use of existing housing stock while protecting people and communities from poor conditions and precarious living arrangements, and it complements the work we’ve already advocated on quality, design and delivery in England.

From my lived experience as a renter in England, private housing can feel like a lottery. Flats that are cold, damp or poorly insulated, with slow repairs and bills that bite because the heating is old or inefficient, aren’t acceptable as a norm for a generation trying to get a foothold. Any package of changes needs to secure safer, healthier homes while keeping the private rental market viable. Here’s what I think would work best: 

- Enforceable safety, habitability and energy standards with funded retrofit support
  - Set higher, enforceable safety and habitability standards for all private rentals. This should cover mandatory annual gas safety checks, reliable electrical safety tests, working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in every home, and robust damp and mould remediation responsibilities. Fire safety in blocks should be routinely audited, with clear penalties for non-compliance.
  - Raise energy performance targets and make energy efficiency improvements a condition of lettings. Landlords should aim for a minimum EPC rating and, where feasible, upgrade insulation, windows, heating systems and ventilation. Crucially, this must come with practical retrofit funding: a government-backed grant or voucher scheme that landlords can access without compromising the cash-flow of the tenancy. The savings from lower energy bills should be passed on to renters, not kept as landlord profit.
  - Create a simple, independent mechanism to check delivery against commitments. A lightweight but robust enforcement route should exist, with the ability to issue penalties, require remedial works within set deadlines, and claw back public subsidies if promised improvements aren’t delivered.

- Targeted, practical support for vulnerable renters
  - Strengthen anti-discrimination enforcement and ensure that reasonable adjustments are available for disabled tenants. This should include guidance for prospective renters on accessibility features, and incentives for landlords to adapt existing homes where feasible.
  - Improve tailored support for groups that often face barriers in the private market, including BAME, older and younger renters. This could involve coordinated tenancy advocacy services, translation and signposting, and targeted dispute resolution channels to prevent eviction spirals when households are struggling with repairs or energy costs.
  - Require proactive accessibility information in listings and tenancy documents, so people can assess suitability before applying, reducing the stress of moving into unsuitable homes.

- Security and affordability alongside market sustainability
  - Stabilise rents without stifling supply by offering longer, secure tenancies and predictable rent review paths. Where possible, cap excessive rent increases and tie adjustments to local living standards and energy savings rather than speculative markets.
  - Expand deposit protections and consider deposit-free options or government-backed deposit guarantees to lower upfront barriers, especially for younger renters who are just starting out.
  - Support the market with fair-win policies for small landlords who invest in improvements. Simple, low-cost finance or non-profit backed loans for essential safety and energy upgrades can help small landlords compete with larger operators who have deeper pockets.
  - Increase transparency in how landlords meet these standards. A public dashboard showing compliance rates, average repair times, and energy retrofit activity would help renters hold landlords to account and inform policy adjustments over time.

- Real-world examples and pace of delivery
  - In my town, several flats have persistent damp and a boiler that costs a small fortune to run. An accessible retrofit fund could cover insulation and an efficient heat source, which would not only improve health and comfort but cut bills so much that rent remains affordable in practice. An independent inspectorate with real penalties for non-delivery would also deter the pattern of delayed repairs that pushes people into worse living situations while waiting for a landlord’s “maintenance window.”
  - I’ve seen how targeted support for vulnerable renters can change outcomes: translation services at housing offices, dedicated advocacy when disputes arise, and clearer guidance on what reasonable adjustments look like in practice all reduce eviction risk and help people stay housed with dignity.

Balancing ambition with practicality is essential. The changes I’ve outlined aim to raise standards and reduce bills for private renters, especially the most vulnerable, without squeezing landlords out of the market or slowing down the supply of homes. If policymakers couple enforceable, well-funded retrofit and safety requirements with strong anti-discrimination measures and accessible support, we can build a private rental sector that is both fair and sustainable for my generation.

Thank you for considering the lived experience of young people trying to put down roots in our communities.

Private renters need security, decent living conditions and fair costs, without harming the viability of the market. I back stronger local enforcement, clearer landlord responsibilities and meaningful sanctions for failing to meet standards. At the same time we must strengthen support for vulnerable tenants and make accessibility a default, not an afterthought. For example, anti‑discrimination protections should be robust and backed by accessible channels for vulnerable renters such as disabled, older, BAME and young households. Landlords should be required to provide reasonable adjustments and accessibility features where needed, without fear of losing the tenancy. 

Key changes I’d like to see include: expanded enforcement powers for local authorities, with mandatory property inspections in higher‑risk areas and clear penalties (fines or banning orders) for non‑compliance; proactive licensing where appropriate to raise overall standards; and stronger protections around safety and energy efficiency, with practical support to upgrade properties where needed. Tenants should have better access to independent redress, clear deposit protections, and information that is easy to understand. 

These steps must accompany a sustainable market approach: incentives for longer tenancies and professional management, transparent rent information, and targeted funding or relief for landlords upgrading older stock. Taken together, this can raise security, affordability and standards without undermining the private rented sector’s future.

it's outrageous that from my experience renting near Belfast, rents are rising fast and getting repairs done can take too long. To improve security, affordability and standards without undermining the rental market, I’d back a practical mix of stronger local enforcement and sensible landlord support. Key steps:
- Increase local inspection powers and meaningful sanctions for persistent non‑compliance, including timely remediation orders and targeted penalties where safety or health standards aren’t met.
- Require clearer tenancy terms, longer tenancies by default, and faster dispute resolution so renters feel secure and can budget with some depreciation protection against unfair rent hikes between fixed terms.
- Strengthen energy and safety standards with easier access to grants and phased obligations for small landlords so upgrades don’t push them out of the market.
- Expand anti‑discrimination protections and ensure adaptations are funded for disabled, older or vulnerable renters; include tailored support for BAME and younger tenants who may face extra barriers.
- Improve transparency: a public register of planning obligations and delivery milestones, so affordable homes and infrastructure are actually delivered.
- Pilot these reforms in a few councils first, with clear metrics on supply, maintenance times, and tenant satisfaction, before broader rollout.
Overall, a balanced approach—tough enforcement where needed, targeted landlord support, and strong protections for tenants—will help security and standards without sacrificing supply.

From my experience living in England, private renters often face insecurity and variable quality, especially older or disabled tenants and those from minority backgrounds. To improve security, affordability and standards while keeping a sustainable market, I’d push for a package that strengthens fairness, accessibility and targeted support.

- Stronger anti-discrimination enforcement: landlords and letting agents must not refuse housing or impose harsher conditions based on protected characteristics; clearer penalties and mandatory training for those involved in letting. In my area I’ve seen occasional biased treatment that erodes trust in renting.
- Accessibility adaptations: tenants should be able to request reasonable adaptations without barriers, with funding or grants available to cover costs; faster decisions from local authorities and clearer processes for shared spaces.
- Tailored support for vulnerable renters: accessible advocacy, tenancy coaching, and targeted help for disabled, older, young and low-income renters to navigate deposits, larger bills and repairs.
- Security of tenure: longer assured shorthold tenancies with clearer renewal rights and fair eviction protections, so households can plan for the long term.
- Affordability and deposits: cap rent increases in line with inflation, simplify deposits or provide deposit-free options, and improve transparency around pricing.
- Standards: enforce higher energy efficiency (minimum EPC), timely damp/mould remediation and regular safety checks; support for heat and insulation upgrades where needed.
- Landlord responsibilities and enforcement: targeted licensing in high-risk areas and robust enforcement against rogue landlords.
- Data and accountability: regular reporting on discrimination, repairs, and outcomes for vulnerable renters to inform policy improvements.

From my experience in England, improving security and standards for private renters must go hand in hand with maintaining a healthy market. I would support compulsory landlord and agent registration, licensing, and mandatory training or accreditation. A simple, nationwide framework could filter out rogue operators, shine a light on poor property management, and ensure agents understand tenancy law, repairs, deposits and energy efficiency. For instance, in our area a family faced prolonged damp and delayed repairs, while their agent charged high admin fees; a robust licensing scheme would help prevent such experiences.

We should strengthen grounds for eviction and notice rights to curb no-fault and retaliatory evictions. That means longer, clearer notices (4-6 months where possible) and robust appeal rights, with fast-track mediation for disputes. This protects tenants while allowing legitimate landlord needs to be addressed.

Finally, linchpins: anti-discrimination, accessibility adaptations, and targeted support for vulnerable renters. Require reasonable adjustments for disabled tenants; ensure new lets meet accessible standards where feasible; track and tackle discrimination by race, age, or other protected characteristics, and provide targeted help for BAME, older, and younger renters. Any framework must include exemptions for smaller landlords and stay focused on improving quality without choking the supply.

To improve security, affordability and standards for private renters while keeping a sustainable market, I would back compulsory landlord and agent registration, licensing and mandatory training or accreditation. A robust scheme would raise management and compliance standards, weed out the worst operators, and make safety checks (gas/electric) and energy efficiency obligations easier to enforce. It should be simple to join, low-cost for honest landlords, and include exemptions for those who consistently meet high standards. In my area, a couple of landlords maintain older terraces well, but others neglect repairs; registration and accreditation would help tenants know who they are dealing with and provide a clear route for complaints. Importantly, penalties must be proportionate and enforcement targeted at the bad actors, not at small, compliant landlords. I also think strengthening anti-discrimination protections and providing accessibility adaptations with tailored support for disabled, older, BAME and other vulnerable renters would improve outcomes without unduly increasing costs for tenants. And promote minimum or multi-year tenancies with easier renewals to reduce churn, while ensuring fair renewals and transparent rent reviews. A combination of licensing, better standards, longer tenancies and targeted support offers security and affordability while sustaining the private rented sector.

absolutely introduce stronger local enforcement, more frequent inspections, and meaningful sanctions for failing landlords; couple this with clear tenant rights and adequate council funding so standards stay high without harming rental supply!

Two changes would do most to improve security, affordability and standards for private renters while keeping a sustainable market. First, fast, low‑cost tribunals and mediation, backed by funded tenant advice services, so issues can be resolved without fear of reprisals. In our area, tenants often endure damp or long repair delays and worry about eviction if they raise concerns; accessible support helps people know their rights and keeps landlords accountable. Second, to boost affordable supply, push planning reform and incentives for build‑to‑rent with durable affordability covenants and professional management, plus a focus on brownfield development and expansion of social housing. Build‑to‑rent can help, but only if rents are transparent and long‑term affordability is guaranteed with strong stewardship. We also need decent‑homes standards and clear expectations for energy efficiency and timely repairs. Any growth should be underpinned by public or community involvement to ensure long‑term stewardship and real community benefit, not short‑term churn.

From my experience as a renter and student in England, the best way to improve security, affordability and standards without squeezing supply is to couple tenancy reforms with strong energy and development standards. Key ideas I’d back are:
- Longer, easier-to-renew tenancies: minimum 2–3 year leases with straightforward renewal rights to reduce churn, moving costs and help neighbours build stable communities.
- Coordinated development: new private rental schemes should be planned alongside transport, schools, healthcare and utilities, with realistic developer contributions via planning obligations to fund local services and infrastructure.
- Energy efficiency as standard: a fabric-first approach for new homes and a clear path to low-carbon heating, plus a national retrofit fund to upgrade insulation, windows and heating in older stock. This lowers bills for renters and makes homes healthier.
- Affordability safeguards: transparent rent review rules tied to inflation or income, plus deposit reform to reduce upfront costs while maintaining landlord protections.
- Support for small landlords: public guarantees and affordable loans to upgrade properties and manage risk, ensuring quality homes don’t vanish from the market.
- Tenant protections and fast repairs: clear maintenance standards, responsive service and safeguards against harassment. These steps together can keep a sustainable, high-quality private rental sector.

From my perspective as someone living in England and in the 55-64 age bracket, I think a careful mix of registration, enforcement and targeted standards is needed to improve private renting without choking the market. Introduce compulsory landlord and letting-agent registration, licensing and mandatory training or accreditation. A public, easily searchable register would help tenants verify who owns or manages a property and whether they meet basic standards. In practice, I’ve heard of properties managed by unscrupulous agents who delay repairs and dodge safety checks; stronger registration and a code of practice would raise the baseline.

But registration must be paired with real enforcement. Councils need more powers and funding to inspect properties, enforce improvements and apply meaningful sanctions—fines, licence suspensions or revocation—for persistent non-compliance. Sanctions should be proportionate and directed at the landlord, not the tenant, to protect rights and keep the market viable.

And we must raise standards. Set enforceable safety, habitability and energy-efficiency standards, with funded retrofit support so landlords can afford improvements. Grants or low-interest loans would help small landlords upgrade damp, heating and insulation and raise EPC ratings. Use licensing fees to fund inspections and retrofit support, so the system is self-sustaining.

Taken together, these steps would improve security and standards for private renters while keeping a healthy, sustainable rental market.

There is a strong case for backing small private landlords to improve security, affordability and standards, while steering away from speculative practices that destabilise the market. I’d support a package of targeted measures:
- Tax and incentives: introduce a graduated relief or credit for landlords who offer long‑term, affordable tenancies and meet safety and energy standards, paired with a modest stamp duty surcharge on additional properties used for investment. Exempt genuine resident landlords and those operating at a small scale to avoid harming supply.
- Mortgage support: provide government‑backed guarantees or preferential financing for lenders who refinance portfolios to keep rents affordable and fund required safety and energy upgrades.
- Standards and retrofit: set enforceable safety, habitability and energy‑efficiency standards with funded retrofit support so tenants pay less energy and enjoy safer homes. Expand grants/loans for alarms, CO detectors, insulation and efficient heating systems.
- Tenancy stability: encourage longer, clearly documented tenancies with reliable repairs responsibilities and timely enforcement.
In practice, I know a local small landlord who kept rents reasonable and upgraded properties when helped by retrofit grants. If such targeted support is available, a sustainable private rented sector can protect tenants and still attract responsible landlords.

From my experience in England, private renters often face insecurity because tenancy lengths are short and renewals uncertain. Introducing minimum lengths of 2-3 years with simpler renewal processes would reduce churn, cut moving costs, and help families feel rooted in their communities. Importantly, increases in rent should be fair and predictable, guided by transparent benchmarks to prevent unaffordable spikes.

Standards: local councils need stronger enforcement powers and meaningful sanctions for rogue landlords. In our town there are damp and heating faults that linger because inspections carry limited consequences. Better inspection regimes, timely repairs, and penalties for non-compliance would raise living standards and protect tenants.

Housing support: reform Local Housing Allowance to reflect current local rents. I know a family who fell into arrears after LHA shortfalls and nearly lost their home; aligning benefits with local rents would reduce arrears and homelessness risk.

Sustainable market: require energy efficiency upgrades and clear obligations for landlords; well-maintained, energy-efficient homes are cheaper to run and more attractive to tenants, supporting affordability in the long term.

All changes should be paired with delivery of local services and infrastructure alongside new housing, ensuring the area can absorb growth without compromising quality of life.

In Scotland, private renters deserve security, clearer standards and affordability, without losing a sustainable market. Two changes would make a real difference. First, reform Local Housing Allowance and housing benefit interactions so they reflect local rents. In my area, LHA rates barely keep pace with private rents, leaving households in arrears and at risk of homelessness. I’d back an automatic uplift tied to local market rents, for example targeting at least the 30th percentile of current local rents, with a simple index linked to local rents and CPI. Faster, simpler housing benefit decisions and payments are essential too, so landlords are paid on time and tenants aren’t exposed to avoidable arrears. This approach would stabilise households, reduce eviction risk and keep a healthier rental market. Second, curb short‑term lets and second homes to protect long‑term rental stock. Local licensing or caps would ensure communities aren’t hollowed out by high turnover; licences should require safety standards, proper taxation, and a share of receipts reinvested in local affordable housing or enforcement. I’ve seen properties convert to holiday lets, squeezing long‑term supply; with targeted enforcement and fair enforcement funding, we can protect tenants while remaining attractive for visitors.

To improve security, affordability and standards for private renters while keeping the market sustainable, we must boost the supply of good homes and ensure high, enforceable standards. Planning reform should unlock brownfield land in town and district centres for purpose-built private rental and build-to-rent schemes, to relieve pressure on existing stock and help keep rents in check. Well‑managed BTR developments often offer longer tenancies and professional maintenance, which suits many of us who value stability without sacrificing choice.

Incentivising build-to-rent with grants or targeted tax relief for schemes that include genuinely affordable options, plus strong energy efficiency commitments, would accelerate decent, modern homes without sidelining smaller investors. Expanding social housing and making sensible use of public land for affordable rental would also help free up private homes for longer tenancies.

On standards, mandatory licensing and robust enforcement must continue, paired with ambitious energy upgrades—better insulation, heating, and lower-energy heating systems funded by low-interest loans or grants. I’ve seen damp flats in my area; stronger enforcement and accessible upgrades would make a real difference. Pair longer, fair rent reviews with rent stability measures as supply grows, not at the expense of tenants. Taken together, these changes support security now and a sustainable private rented sector for the future.

Enable security and standards by fast, low-cost tribunals, funded tenant advice and mediation, so issues resolve without fear. Boost supply via planning reform, Build-to-Rent incentives, brownfield development, and social housing expansion; keep rent stability through longer tenancies and clear, enforced standards for repairs and energy efficiency.

To improve security, affordability and standards for private renters without stifling the market, I support longer, clearer tenancies and simpler renewals. In my experience living in Wales, leases tend to roll over yearly, which means moving costs, disrupted schooling for kids, and weaker community ties. A baseline tenancy of at least two to three years with automatic renewal unless the tenant chooses to end would stabilise households and help families plan.

Pair this with predictable, capped rent increases tied to CPI plus a modest margin so budgets aren’t blown apart at every renewal. Ensure strong minimum standards: timely repairs, safe, energy-efficient homes (better EPCs and upgrades funded by landlords or grants), and a clear, fast route for disputes Obviously.... Tenants should have affordable, quick access to deposit protection schemes and fair methods for renewals.

Protect tenants from retaliatory evictions and require landlords to provide transparent, up-to-date information on property condition and compliance. For sustainability, offer targeted support to landlords to upgrade older properties rather than driving supply away. These changes would stabilise communities, improve living standards, and maintain a viable private rental market in Wales.

Agree: compulsory landlord/agent registration, licensing, and mandatory accreditation training would raise management standards, improve tenant security, support fair rents, and help sustain a sustainable private rental market.

From my experience in Scotland, the private rented sector works best when safety, predictability and value are built in, not patching up problems after they appear. The changes that would have the biggest impact are three linked steps. 

First, empower local authorities with stronger enforcement and meaningful sanctions. Councils need robust inspection powers over disrepair, safety standards and energy efficiency, with clear, enforceable deadlines for fixes and penalties that deter the worst practices. Publishing performance data and offering targeted grants or low‑interest loans to help landlords upgrade where needed would drive genuine improvement while keeping maintenance costs manageable. 

Second, provide fast, low‑cost tribunals, mediation and funded tenant advisory services so issues can be resolved quickly and without fear of reprisal. In practice this means digital case handling, reduced or waived fees for renters, and funded advice services that help tenants understand rights and negotiate. 

Third, increase affordable supply by planning reform and incentives for build‑to‑rent, brownfield development and social housing expansion. Streamlined planning for well‑managed BTR with affordability covenants, together with use of public land for social housing, can deliver steadier, longer‑term rents aligned with local earnings. 

These measures together can raise standards, cut insecurity and keep a sustainable market.

Agree, and I think the changes should be practical and locally enforceable. In my experience as an older resident, gaps in enforcement mean damp, unsafe homes and repairs that take too long. To improve security, affordability and standards:
- Give councils stronger powers to inspect private rentals, require timely repairs, and apply meaningful sanctions for unsafe homes or poor management. A property with repeated issues should face escalating penalties or licence review, and tenants must have a clear route to complain.
- Introduce compulsory landlord and agent registration and licensing, with mandatory training or accreditation. A public register would help tenants avoid rogue operators and raise overall management standards.
- Design tax, mortgage and incentive measures to protect small landlords' viability while discouraging speculative and large-scale exits. For example, targeted relief for compliant landlords who invest in energy efficiency and repairs, paired with measures to curb large portfolios that push up rents or withdraw supply.
- Extend protections that matter most to tenants: cap letting agent fees, require up-to-date gas safety and carbon monoxide detectors, and set reasonable repair timelines.
Pilot these approaches in a few councils, with robust monitoring on landlords, supply and tenant outcomes.

From where I sit, owning a warm, safe home has never felt more essential than in retirement. I’ve spent most of my life in England watching rents creep up, while maintenance and safety standards in some private rental homes lag behind what families can reasonably expect. My experience and conversations with neighbours make me think there’s a straightforward way to improve security, affordability and standards for private renters without destabilising the market: compulsory registration and licensing for landlords and agents, backed by mandatory training and accreditation. This would raise the bar across the board, while leaving room for responsible small-scale landlords who provide decent homes already.

First, a unified compulsory registration system for landlords and letting agents is overdue. Landlords should be required to register with a single, national database, providing accurate contact details and a clear record of how many properties they rent. Letting agents would be registered too, so tenants know who is accountable. This isn’t about increasing bureaucracy for its own sake; it’s about making it easier for tenants to report problems and for councils to take swift action when standards slip. In practice, I’ve seen cases where a landlord’s contact details change and repairs suddenly stall. A transparent register would make it harder for unscrupulous actors to hide and would empower tenants to seek help more quickly.

Second, property-level licensing should accompany registration. Each let property would need a licence, with checks covering essential safety standards (gas and electrical safety, smoke and carbon monoxide detectors) and a minimum baseline of home condition. Some properties in my community have good energy efficiency and solid repairs, but others fall well short and the tenants bear the cost of heat and damp. A licence system would create a real incentive for landlords to keep properties in decent shape and to respond promptly to repair requests, since licences would require renewal and could be revoked for persistent breach.

Third, mandatory training or accreditation for landlords and letting agents. Legal obligations around tenancy rights, deposits, repairs, and fair dealing should not be left to chance. Accredited training would cover, for example, how to handle deposits responsibly, how to provide clear, transparent tenancy information, and what vulnerable tenants are entitled to. It would also include practical guidance on energy efficiency improvements and cost-effective heating solutions, so older renters aren’t trapped in cold flats. For smaller landlords, there should be subsidised or low-cost routes to accreditation to avoid pricing them out of the market.

Fourth, strengthen and standardise deposit protection and dispute resolution. Tenants are most exposed at the start and end of tenancies. A robust deposit protection scheme, with swift, independent dispute resolution, would reduce disputes and give tenants confidence that their money is safe and returned when deserved. In my street, a delayed deposit return caused real anxiety for a family moving out after several years; a clearer framework would have spared that worry.

Fifth, ban or curb excessive letting fees and require transparent billing. Tenants should not be hit with surprise charges for referencing, admin, or renewal. Clear, itemised statements should be the norm, with caps on certain charges where appropriate. This helps keep private renting affordable and predictable, which matters greatly when energy bills and groceries are eating into fixed incomes.

Sixth, tie the standards to practical enforcement. Licences would be granted only if the property passes safety checks and meets minimum housing conditions. Local authorities would have powers to suspend or revoke licences, issue improvement notices, and levy penalties for serious or repeated breaches. The goal is not to punish landlords but to protect tenants and create a level playing field where well-run units thrive and poorly managed ones face consequences.

Seventh, protect sustainable supply. I recognise that over-regulating could drive some landlords out of the market, so exemptions should exist for genuine small-scale landlords who maintain good standards and engage constructively. For those, lighter-touch routes to accreditation could be offered, with additional support and guidance. Revenue from registration and licensing should fund enforcement and high-quality training, not become a new source of tax.

Finally, give tenants real, accessible routes to complain and seek remedy. A user-friendly national helpline, an online portal with clear guidance, and a simple process to escalate urgent safety issues would make a tangible difference, especially for older residents who may be less confident dealing with problem properties.

These changes would raise security, improve living standards, and help keep private renting a sustainable part of the housing market. They would complement the broader reforms I’ve favoured—diversifying who delivers housing, tying housing more closely to services, and insisting on timely infrastructure alongside new homes. Private renters deserve warm, safe homes with predictable costs and reliable repairs; licensing, registration and training for landlords and agents are practical steps toward that goal.

Private renters need a system that protects security, maintains decent standards and keeps rents affordable without stifling investment. Two linked changes would help. First, any new private rental development should be tightly coordinated with transport, schools, GP surgeries and utilities, with realistic, enforceable developer contributions. Too many schemes add homes but leave communities with clogged roads, inadequate local services and unreliable energy infrastructure. I’d insist on an explicit infrastructure package attached to planning approvals, plus targets for genuinely affordable private rental components and energy efficiency upgrades in every property. Second, strengthen tenancy protections to curb no-fault and retaliatory evictions and improve security. Longer, clearer notice periods and robust, time-limited grounds for eviction would reduce sudden displacement. Tenants must have an accessible route to raise disrepair or safety concerns without fear of retaliation, with swift penalties for abuse. In my area, a block near the station had decent rents but very poor energy efficiency; when tenants complained about mould, some were served notices to leave. These protections, paired with responsible development, would stabilise the market and support sustainable growth.

Thank you for the opportunity to feed in on how we can improve security, affordability and standards for private renters without undermining a sustainable rental market. My experience in England over the past few years has shown rents rising faster than wages, with families understandably feeling squeezed, and some landlords struggling to justify ongoing upgrades when returns are under pressure. I believe a carefully balanced package, combining targeted support for small landlords with reform of housing-benefit interactions, can deliver safer, more affordable homes while keeping the private rented sector viable.

First, in ensuring the sector remains financially workable for small landlords who provide the majority of private rental homes, I would like to see a package of tax, mortgage and incentive measures that rewards responsible, long‑term renting and discourages speculative or large‑scale exits. On tax and incentives, a targeted relief for genuine maintenance and safety improvements would be invaluable. For example, allowing deductions or credits for essential repairs, safety upgrades and energy-efficiency work could encourage landlords to raise standards without driving up rents unnecessarily. It would help if these incentives were time-limited but predictable, so landlords could plan and invest with confidence.

On mortgages, I’d welcome government‑backed options that support landlords who participate in longer tenancies and keep properties well maintained. Measures could include more accessible financing terms for properties that are rented at stable, affordable levels and meet minimum safety and energy standards, provided the landlord demonstrates a commitment to long‑term tenancy. This would stabilise cash flow for small landlords facing rising costs and help them resist the impulse to exit the market when faced with short‑term rent pressure.

To discourage speculative activity and large‑scale exits, I’d support a light‑touch framework that creates positive incentives for staying invested in the private rented sector and maintaining homes to a high standard, while imposing sensible consequences for behaviour that reduces stock or quality. For instance, landlords who commit to a minimum number of years of tenancy, maintain properties to a defined standard and invest in energy upgrades could receive ongoing relief or priority access to affordable financing. Conversely, a broad incentive or levy could apply to firms that frequently flip properties or convert entire portfolios to short‑lets or non‑tenancy uses, reflecting the costs these practices impose on local housing supply and tenants.

Secondly, reforming Local Housing Allowance and housing-benefit interactions is essential to reduce arrears, homelessness risk and reputational damage to landlords who do the right thing. I would support implementing LHA that reflects local rents more accurately, with quarterly updates tied to the actual rental market in each area. This would make benefit support more predictable for tenants and more stable for landlords relying on timely payments.

In practical terms, this could involve:
- Calculating LHA levels using local median rents for the relevant bedroom category, with automatic uplifts when local rents rise and a simple mechanism for councils to adjust more quickly during market shocks. This reduces the mismatch that currently pushes households into arrears.
- Increasing Discretionary Housing Payments allocations so councils can top up households most at risk of arrears or homelessness, and ensuring quick, direct payments to landlords when appropriate to keep tenancies intact.
- Streamlining interactions between housing benefit, universal credit and private landlords, including clearer guidance and simpler processes for direct payments where tenancy risk is high, so tenants and landlords experience fewer payment delays.
- Protecting tenants during transitions and ensuring that improvements in local rent data translate into better protection against homelessness for those most at risk.

These LHA reforms would sit alongside the better enforcement of quality standards I mentioned earlier. It should be a package that provides tenants with steadier payments and predictable housing costs, while ensuring landlords receive timely rent where properties meet decent standards and energy efficiency targets.

In sum, the changes I’d prioritise are a balanced set of measures that support small landlords who keep rents affordable and properties well-maintained, coupled with reform of housing-benefit interactions to align with local markets and reduce arrears. This combination would help security for tenants, improve standards and energy efficiency, and maintain a sustainable, diverse private rented sector rather than a volatile, landlord-exit market. I’ve seen both the good landlords do—investing in better homes—and the risks when policy levers do not align with market realities; a coordinated approach can deliver better outcomes for families and for those who invest responsibly in rented housing.

From my experience as a renter in England, I see real value in raising management and compliance standards. Making landlor and letting agent registration mandatory, with a public licensing scheme and required training, could lift security, make rent more predictable, and reduce disputes. A central, searchable register would help tenants check who they are dealing with and enable quicker action when things go wrong. Licensing could require landlords to meet basic safety standards, complete regular gas and electrical checks, and demonstrate energy efficiency improvements. Training or accreditation for agents would coverr tenancy rights, deposits, repairs, and prohibited practices, giving trnants clearer routes to complain. But it must be designed to avoid squeezing small landlords or reducing supply. Propose tiered licensing or exemptions for landlords with a small portfolio, and a phased rollout focused first on higher-risk areas or larger properties. Funds from licensing fees should fund enforcement and tenant advisory services,, not create bureaucracy. Tie the regime to existing protections: tenancy deposit schemes, minimum energy performance standards, and planned energy-efficiency upgrades. Overall, I support moves to improve security and standards for private renters, provided the system is affordable to landlords, well-enforced, and evaluated to ensure it helps rather than harms a sustainable rental market.

To improve security, affordability and standards for private renters while keeping a sustainable market, policy should prioritise small landlords and ordinary tenants, not just big investors. This means targeted tax, mortgage and incentive measures that keep small portfolios viable while discouraging speculative buying and large-scale exits. Reward landlords who offer longer tenancies, invest in energy efficiency and keep rents affordable relative to local incomes. Local Housing Allowance must reflect what rents actually cost here. In practice, uprating LHA to local market levels, ensuring timely benefit payments, and providing arrears protection would reduce evictions and homelessness risk. In my area, delays in benefit payments have pushed households toward arrears; faster, more predictable support would stabilise tenancies and keep rents affordable.

Finally, expand affordable supply through planning reform and targeted incentives for build-to-rent, brownfield redevelopment and social housing growth. Easier, faster planning for small-scale schemes and mandatory inclusion of affordable homes in new builds would create more secure private rentals without crowding out social housing. A balanced package like this supports long-term tenancies, steadier rents and better quality standards.

To improve security, affordability and standards in private renting while keeping a sustainable market, three measures are needed. Firstly, increase affordable supply through planning reform and targeted incentives for build-to-rent, brownfield development and expansion of social housing. More affordable, well-located homes would reduce pressure on rents and cut churn, something I’ve seen firsthand in Scotland where good-quality options are scarce and moving costs bite. Secondly, promote longer tenancies and simpler renewals to stabilise households and strengthen community ties. When people can count on a stable home, they invest in their neighbourhood, not just pack up every year. Thirdly, strengthen eviction safeguards: longer, clearer notice periods, robust grounds for eviction, and fair appeal rights to curb no-fault and retaliatory evictions. And underpin all that with firm standards—decent repairs, energy efficiency, and safety checks—so that added security and supply don’t come at the expense of quality. To improve security, affordability and standards for private renters while keeping a sustainable market, the focus should be on reforming Local Housing Allowance and how housing benefit interacts with local rents. LHA should be tied to credible local rent data and updated regularly, so rates reflect what rents actually are in my area. When LHA lags behind market rents, arrears grow and families risk homelessness; I’ve seen neighbours fall into difficulty because benefits didn’t keep pace with rent increases.

I’d also simplify and speed up claims, and ensure landlords receive timely payments. Direct payments to the landlord must continue when tenants are delayed, and the system should be designed to avoid unnecessary evictions. Ensure access to support to prevent arrears, including clear guidance and local help desks.

On standards, require better energy efficiency, regular safety checks, and stronger enforcement against poorly maintained properties. Licensing for private landlords in high-demand areas, with ring-fenced funds to improve housing stock and energy efficiency, would help.

Finally, promote reasonable tenancy security, such as longer fixed-term agreements where possible, with rents aligned to local inflation, so households can stay put without risking affordability.

From my perspective as a long-standing resident in England, I want a private rented sector that is safer, more affordable and better maintained, but I also want to keep a healthy supply of homes so our area doesn’t lose private rentals altogether. That means careful, targeted reforms rather than blunt, broad caps that could push good landlords out of the market. Here are the changes I think would work best, drawn from what I’ve seen locally and what’s worked in other parts of the country when properly applied.

Security of tenure and fair handling of evictions
- Encourage longer, simple tenure options by default (for example, two to three-year initial tenancies with automatic renewal unless there are clear, justified reasons for ending the contract). This would give households—particularly older residents like me’s peers—a stable home without locking landlords into unprofitable arrangements.
- Tighten protections against no-fault evictions and ensure eviction grounds are clear, timely, and fair. Tenants should have a dependable process to challenge unfair practice, with independent, accessible help if problems arise.
- Strengthen deposit protection and provide fast, transparent redress for disputes about repairs or damages. A simple, trusted pathway reduces disputes and keeps tenancy relationships constructive.

Standards, safety and energy efficiency
- Raise and enforce minimum standards for repairs and safety, with a robust inspection regime. As a renter, you shouldn’t have to live with damp, mold, or broken heating mid-winter.
- Accelerate energy efficiency improvements by offering affordable financing or subsidies to landlords who upgrade. A more energy-efficient home is not only better for the environment; it keeps bills down for tenants and makes renting more affordable overall.
- Require regular safety checks (gas, electrical) with clear timelines for remediation and penalties for non-compliance funded by the enforcement system rather than passed onto tenants.

Affordability without harming supply
- Instead of broad rent caps, implement targeted subsidies and stabilisation mechanisms that help households with the sharpest affordability pressures while preserving landlord returns and the supply chain.
- If caps are considered, they should be tightly targeted and time-limited, tied to local CPI growth with a modest floor and ceiling (for example, CPI plus a small margin, with exemptions for new-builds and major upgrades). This approach discourages rapid price hikes while avoiding a disincentive for landlords to rent out or improve properties.
- Expand and simplify access to subsidies for private renters who need help with rents, such as extending and adapting Local Housing Allowance or comparable vouchers, so landlords can reliably expect payment when they rent to households with limited incomes.
- Create or enlarge incentive schemes for landlords who keep rents affordable long-term (for example, tax relief or longer-term tenancy bonuses for those who commit to capped or affordable rents in specific areas).

Transparency, accountability and data
- Require a public-facing dashboard for the private rented sector at local levels, showing average rents, vacancy rates, compliance with safety and energy standards, and the speed of repair works. Local councils can use this to target interventions where they’re most needed and to hold rogue or unresponsive landlords to account.
- Establish a central, searchable register of landlords and licenses that makes it easier for tenants to verify standards and for authorities to tackle non-compliance quickly.
- Encourage landlords who invest in quality, well-maintained homes to publish key metrics (energy rating, average time to complete repairs, complaint outcomes) so tenants can make informed choices and bad practice is deterred through reputational pressure.

Local flexibility and a plan that supports supply
- Allow councils to tailor policies to their market conditions, with rigorous evaluation requirements so we can learn what actually works and scale it where effective.
- Tie reforms to supply-side benefits: support conversion of suitable empty space into housing, simple, fast-track planning for well-designed refurbishments, and targeted support for small landlords and SMEs who disproportionately provide rental stock in towns like ours.
- Maintain green-field protections and local biodiversity commitments, unless there is a strong, demonstrable and time-bound supply benefit that also safeguards quality and tenure security.

Personal reflection and evidence
- In my town, I’ve watched tenants struggle with sudden rent hikes and landlords who delay essential repairs because the penalties for non-compliance are weak or slow to enforce. I’ve also seen some decent landlords who invest in upgrades but feel overwhelmed by red tape. So I’m not against reforms that improve security and standards; I’m against anything that drags on supply or penalises responsible landlords.
- Any policy should come with robust local monitoring and a credible enforcement mechanism funded by the public purse but designed to fund immediate mitigation for tenants (for example, emergency repairs or short-term housing while longer-term improvements are made), not as a windfall for penalties.

Overall, I support changes that lift security, improve standards and help those on lower incomes, but only if they are carefully designed to preserve and sometimes grow supply. A mix of targeted subsidies, sensible tenure protections, stronger standards, and local data-driven enforcement will help make private renting fairer and more predictable without collapsing the market on which many households depend.

Support stronger local enforcement and meaningful sanctions to raise private rental standards, reform Local Housing Allowance to reflect local rents and reduce arrears, and boost supply via planning reform, build-to-rent incentives, brownfield development and social housing expansion.

From my perspective in Scotland, and as someone who would prefer renting to owning for the flexibility and simplicity it offers in later life, the private rental market needs to be fair, predictable and well‑managed. The core of what would improve security, affordability and standards is good, accessible dispute resolution alongside stronger, clear obligations on landlords and professional property management. I’d also like to see a continued, value‑driven role for Build‑to‑Rent schemes with affordability covenants as part of a sustainable market. Here are the changes I think would work best, drawing on what I’ve seen and heard locally.

- Fast, low‑cost tribunals, mediation and funded tenant advice services
  - Create streamlined, inexpensive avenues to resolve issues without fear of reprisals. It would be reassuring if tribunals could offer simplified processes for straightforward matters and quicker decisions in cases of repair delays, improper charges or harassment. I’d like to see funded, independent tenant advice services that can help older renters understand their rights, help complete forms and accompany them to meetings or hearings when needed. This would reduce the burden on individuals and encourage more people to raise genuine concerns.
  - Mediation should be readily available for disputes over repairs, access to common facilities, service charges and lease terms. A lightweight, early‑stage mediation service could prevent small issues from escalating into formal disputes and potential eviction actions.

- Longer security and clearer tenancy rights
  - Encourage longer, secure tenancies with predictable renewals and reasonable rent review processes. While we must avoid stifling supply, stability is crucial for older renters who want to stay in familiar communities and avoid repeated moves.
  - Ensure clear tenancy rights and protections against unfair eviction, with rapid access to independent support if a landlord falls short on obligations.

- Transparent, fair rents and charges
  - Implement transparent rent setting practices with defined review intervals and caps tied to local income or inflation, whichever is lower. In Build‑to‑Rent schemes with covenanted rents, this should be reinforced by professional management to prevent arbitrary increases.
  - Require itemised service charges and provide caps where appropriate. Tenants should have access to independent oversight if charges seem excessive or unclear, and any major works should be pre‑planned with community consultation.

- Standards and maintenance that tenants can trust
  - Enforce minimum repair standards and response times for maintenance requests, with mandatory reporting to the regulator for large landlords and management companies.
  - Require energy efficiency improvements and accessible design where possible, so residents have lower energy bills and comfortable homes in all weathers.
  - Mandate professional on‑site management for larger private developments, ensuring tenants have a single point of contact for repairs, repairs tracking and service information.

- Landlord responsibilities, visible accountability and renter support
  - Deposit protections should be robust and accessible, with quick resolution mechanisms for disputes about return of deposits.
  - Reject unreasonable fees and ensure upfront transparency about all costs associated with tenancy from the outset.
  - Landlords with larger portfolios should appoint a local management company or dedicated on‑site team, making it easier for tenants to raise concerns and get timely responses.

- Sustaining a healthy market alongside Build‑to‑Rent
  - Build‑to‑Rent remains a valuable backbone for secure, well‑managed rental stock. Ensuring a meaningful share of covenanted units and integrated tenancy options (rented, affordable sale, shared ownership) helps communities stay cohesive and affordable over time.
  - Regulators and local authorities should publish performance data on landlord compliance, maintenance turnaround times, and tenant satisfaction. This would help tenants choose responsibly and push underperforming landlords to improve.

In practice, I’ve heard from friends living in well‑run Build‑to‑Rent blocks that having on‑site staff and clear community rules leads to faster repairs, better information flow, and more predictable costs than many scattered private rentals. However, problems still arise when tenants feel there’s little recourse beyond leaving or accepting poor conditions. A system of affordable, accessible advice, quick dispute resolution and stronger upfront standards would make a real difference—especially for older residents who value security, dignity and staying within familiar communities.

If policymakers can deliver these measures—fast, affordable dispute resolution; funded tenant advice; clearer rights and obligations; and a sustainable Build‑to‑Rent framework with covenanted rents and professional management—we can maintain a healthy private rental market that is fair, predictable and decent to live in for decades to come.
