- DEFAULT TO MINIMUM 2–3 YEAR TENANCIES WITH AUTOMATIC RENEWAL, UNLESS THE LANDLORD HAS A CLEAR, JUSTIFIED REASON TO END THE TENANCY. THIS WOULD GIVE HOUSEHOLDS STABILITY TO PLAN AND INVEST IN THEIR HOMES.
- CAP RENT INCREASES AT A SENSIBLE LEVEL (FOR EXAMPLE CPI PLUS A SMALL MARGIN) AND REQUIRE TRANSPARENT, TIMELY JUSTIFICATION FOR ANY RISES. THIS PROTECTS AFFORDABILITY WHILE PRESERVING LANDLORD VIABILITY.
- END NO-FAULT EVICTIONS AND PROVIDE LONGER NOTICE PERIODS (E.G., 6 MONTHS) FOR TENANCY ENDINGS, WITH SAFEGUARDS TO ENSURE LEGITIMATE GROUNDS ARE USED.
- STRENGTHEN RENEWAL SUPPORT: STREAMLINED RENEWAL PROCESSES, PROMPT RESPONSES TO REPAIRS DURING THE TENANCY, AND CLEARER HANDLING OF CHARGES SO TENANTS AREN’T SURPRISED AT RENEWAL.
- RAISE STANDARDS: MANDATE AT LEAST EPC BAND C BY 2035, ANNUAL GAS SAFETY CHECKS, AND TIMELY REPAIRS FOR DAMP, MOULD AND URGENT ISSUES. IMPROVE DEPOSITS SCHEMES AND DISPUTE RESOLUTION TO RESOLVE DISAGREEMENTS FAIRLY.
- ALLOW FOR PRACTICAL FLEXIBILITY: LANDLORDS SHOULD RETAIN A ROUTE TO EXIT FOR MAJOR WORKS OR RESALE, BUT WITH FAIR COMPENSATION AND CLEAR TIMELINES.

THESE MEASURES WOULD IMPROVE SECURITY AND AFFORDABILITY FOR PRIVATE RENTERS WHILE MAINTAINING A SUSTAINABLE, INVESTABLE RENTAL MARKET.

From my position as a pensioner living in England, private renting should be secure, affordable and well managed, but any reforms must avoid placing good landlords under unsustainable burdrn whilee preserving a healthy rental market. Over the years I’ve seen a mix of landlord practices in our area—some diligent and responsive, others slow to act or hard to reach. The right changes could lift standards and tenant security without driving up costs or reducing availablr homes,, but they need careful design, staged rollout and robust enforcement funded from public sources. I would support the following directions, providedd they are implemented with guardrails and evaluation from the outset: - Compulsory landlord/agent registration, licensing and mandatory training or accreditation - This would set a baseline for safety, repairs, and professional conduct. Basic safeguards would include gas and electrical safety compliance,, timely repairs, clear communication, and accessible complaint channels. Licensing could require evidence of energy-efficiency improvements and disability-access considerations where appropriate. - Training or accreditation should cover good management practices, fair dealing, and safeguarding tenants from harassment or discrimination. Fees must be reasonable and proportionate, with exemptions or reduced fres for very small landlords to avoid pushing them out of the market. - Revenue from licensing could finance enforcement, inspector activity, and practical support for landlords to upgrade properties. I’d want transparent, publicly available rrporting on license outcomes, property conditions, and tenant satisfaction to build trust. - In practice, a phased approach or pilots in particular districts would help us see what works best before any national rollout. In my area, a clear, voluntary quality standard already helps tenants identify reliable landlords; formal registration would hopefully widen that assurance to all private rented homes. - Strengthen grounds, notice periods and appeal rights to limit no-fault and retaliatory evictions - Tenants deserve security when they raise repairs, report damp or seek srnsible changes to hteeir home. Extending notice periods to a longer, predictable window (for example, 4–6 months) would reduce sudden displacement and give households time to plan, without removing legitimate landlord needs. - Stronger protections against retaliatory eviction should be in place, with a clea appeals mechanism and independent mediation when disputes arise. This should be paired with a transparent timetable for resolving non-compliance issues, so tenant aren’t left in limbo. - Any restrictions on no-fault evictions must be paired with fair, evidence-based grounds for ending a tenancy in legitimate circumstances (sale, significant refurbishment, move-in requirements) and support for tenants to access temporary or alternative accommodation if needed. - A practical worry is that overly punitive rules could deter landlords from renting and reduce supply. That’s why enforcement and support for compliant landlords—such as guidance, templates for responsive repairs, and access to affordable upgrades—are vital. - Promote minimum or multi-year tenancies and easier renewals to reduce churn, moving costs and support community ties - Fixed terms of two to three years with automatic renewals (unless either party opts out under clear, fair conditions) would stabilise households, especially for retirees who value routines and nearby services. A predictable rent path during renewals—perhaps linkrd to inflation wihte a reasonable cap—could protect both tenants and landlords from volatile changes. - Easier renewal processes, coupled with clear, objective criteria for rent reviews, would reduce the anxiety and costs associated with frequent moves. Deposit protrctions and timely repairs should underpin thes longer tenancies, reinforcing trust. - Of course, landlords must retain legitimate exit routes where investment plans change or property needs major works. The key is balancing security with a workable, transparent framework thatt does not remove the incentive to rent out properties. In addition, any reform should be piloted and evaluated with public data before nationwide rollout. This would include comparing areas with differen licensing requirements, eviction protections, and tenancy durations, and publishing the findings so communities can see what works. Proper funding for enforcement, support services for landlords and tenants, and clear, local delivery plans will be essential. Overall, I believe these changes could raise standards, improve affordability, and strengthen security for private renters while keeping a sustainable rental market. The important caveat is pragmatism: protect responsible landlords, invest in enforcement and training, and ensure reforms are backrd by solid evidence and clear delivery plans.

From my experience in Scotland, the risk to the rental stock comes not from renters asking for higher standards, but from policies that push small landlords out of the market. To improve security, affordability, and standards without shrinking supply, I’d focus on targeted tax, mortgage and incentive measures that protect small landlords and deter speculation. 

- Tax: create a targeted relief or tax credit for landlords with up to four properties to help cover mortgage costs and essential maintenance, while phasing out relief for large-scale or corporate investment.
- Stamp duty and CGT: adjust rules to discourage rapid flipping and non-resident purchasing, but keep a fair route for ordinary buyers.
- Mortgage lending: promote longer, stable fixed-rate products for small landlords and sensible stress-testing, so rising rates don’t trigger mass sales.
- Incentives: provide grants or low-interest loans for energy efficiency upgrades and safety improvements; offer accelerated depreciation for these investments.
- Standards: retain strong safety rules, ensure deposit protection, and offer a clear, affordable compliance timetable with support for small landlords.

In my area, a couple of landlords I know say they’d stay invested if these targeted supports were in place rather than blanket penalties that drive them out. A sustainable rental market needs practical, proportionate measures that protect both tenants and small-scale landlords.

To reinforce a sustainable rental market,, changes to the private rented sector should prioritise security, affordability and higher standards, with a strong focus on accessibility and support for vulnerable tenants. I would push for: - Stronger anti-discrimination enforcement in lettings, with mandatory training for landlords and letting agents on equality, disabilityy rights and cultural awareness, plus clear penalties for harassment or biased practices. - Accessibility adaptations funded by grants or tax relief for landlords who install reasonable changes (step-free access, wider doors, accessible bathrooms) and a streamlined process for tenants to request adaptations via local authorities. - Tailore support for disabled, older, BAME and younger renters, including tenancy coaches or caseworkers to assist with benefits, rights, repairs and lease understanding. - Security of tenure: longer default fixed terms (2-3 years) with meaningful renewal rights and protections against no-fault evictions, balanced by fair processes for essential ends of lets. - Standards and enforcement: mandatory timely repairs, damp/mould rrmediation, and a target EPC Band C for private rentals where feasible; robust deposit protection and regular safety checks. - Local authorities empowered to enforce these standards and fund improvements, while continuing to support supply through good-quality, well-managed private housing. In my experience, a neighbour with mobility issues benefited from a ramp funded after advocacy and council support, illustrating how these changes can work in practice.

From where I sit, the surest way to improve security, affordability and standards for private renters, without risking an erosion of the market, is to push for more affordable supply and to fix how housing benefit interacts with local rents. I’ve seen how delays and gaps in supply push people into poor-quality options or straight into arrears, so reforms must tackle both sides of the equation: more homes to rent and a benefit system that actually covers rents where people live.

Planning reform and targeted incentives to boost supply are essential. There’s real potential in building more purpose‑built private rental and in converting brownfield sites or underused land in towns and city fringes into affordable, well-managed homes. The current planning maze often slows needed development and can leave good sites gathering dust. A clearer, faster pathway—with predictable viability tests, standardised approaches, and upfront expectations about infrastructure—would help developers move projects forward. Incentives for build‑to‑rent could also stabilise tenancies: long-term professional management, quality controls, regular maintenance, and transparent, market-aligned rents. In my area, a brownfield corner near the high street could deliver a few hundred homes if planning blocks were reduced and delivery guaranteed; instead, lengthy approvals have held things up and left locals waiting.

Equally important is expanding social housing alongside private supply. Public land, council-backed schemes, and opportunities to mix tenures on the same sites can deliver stability for households who struggle to keep up with private-sector rents. I’d like to see local authorities empowered to prioritise high‑quality, energy‑efficient builds that meet modern safety standards, with commitments to long-term affordability even when market conditions swing.

Standards must go hand in hand with supply. New-builds should meet high energy and safety standards, and private rentals already in the market should see accessible maintenance, rapid repairs, and robust fire and safety measures. I’d welcome a pathway to raise the minimum energy performance for rentals in a phased, affordable way, plus mandatory gas-safety checks and the installation of safety devices where appropriate. It’s not enough to add stock if tenants are left in draughty, poorly insulated homes with spiralling bills.

On welfare and benefits, reforming Local Housing Allowance to reflect local rents is essential to avoid revolving-door arrears and homelessness risk. In many areas, LHA caps are detached from the real rent levels, which pushes households into arrears or forces them to seek cheaper, poorer-quality accommodation. I’d support linking LHA more closely to actual, local market rents and ensuring that payments reach landlords quickly to prevent eviction or repeated rent arrears. The system should also simplify claims processing, reduce delays, and provide direct payment options that protect both tenants and landlords. A predictable benefit that matches typical local rents would also reduce the fear of moving for work or changing circumstances, which helps keep families in stable housing.

To accompany these reforms, stronger enforcement and clearer protections for tenants are vital. Transparent fees, a commitment to timely repairs, and a credible route to challenge poor management must be in place. Longer tenancy‑security options, with reasonable rent reviews tied to transparent indices, would give tenants real stability without undermining landlords’ ability to manage legitimate costs. Debates about section 21-style reforms are nuanced, but expanding voluntary longer-term tenancies in the private rented sector, where landlords deliver better standards and reliability, would be a positive step.

In short, I believe a combination of boosted supply through planning reform, build‑to‑rent incentives, brownfield and social housing expansion, plus a reformed benefits system that mirrors local rents and reduces arrears, offers the most balanced path. This should be accompanied by robust protections for tenants and clear, enforceable standards for safety and energy efficiency. With effective delivery oversight and regional capacity, these changes could deliver safer, more affordable private renting without sacrificing a sustainable market for landlords and developers alike.

To make private renting safer, fairer and more sustainable, I think a system of compulsory landlord and agent registration, licensing and mandatory training should be introduced. Registration would create a clear map of who is responsible for each let, with a straightforward complaints route and swifter enforcement for rogue practices. In my experience, some tenants struggle to get repairs done or to know who to contact; licensed agents would raise accountability and professional standards, reducing disputes. 

Local councils should have powers to cap or license holiday lets to protect long‑term rental availability and communities, especially in towns where a handful of properties can distort the market. This helps ensure families and younger people can access decent homes rather than being priced out by short-term occupancy. 

Finally, set enforceable safety, habitability and energy efficiency standards, paired with funded retrofit support so landlords can bring properties up to standard without undermining their finances. That would lower bills for tenants, improve health and safety, and support a sustainable, high-quality rental market.

Require longer, secure private tenancies; cap deposits; crack down on discrimination; mandate accessible adaptations and reasonable adjustments; raise minimum energy efficiency to EPC C; offer targeted support for disabled, older, BAME and vulnerable renters; incentivise landlords to maintain affordable, well-maintained homes.

Strengthen local enforcement with universal landlord licensing, regular inspections, and meaningful sanctions for unsafe or poorly managed properties; pair this with clear tenant rights to improve security and standards while keeping a sustainable private rented sector.

Agree that security, affordability and standards rise if new private rentals come with longer tenancies and deposit protections, clearer rights, and higher energy and accessibility standards, while ensuring development is coordinated with transport, schools, healthcare and utilities through realistic developer contributions.

Private renters rightly want security, affordable rents and decent standards, but we must avoid policies that shrink the number of homes available to rent. In my experience, the best approach is to improve energy efficiency and safety while giving tenants reliable, longer-term tenure. Key changes: enforce MEES and raise the bar on energy performance for all rental homes, with clear timelines and penalties for non-compliance; offer grants or vouchers to landlords for insulation, efficient heating, and draught proofing so bills come down rather than rents simply rising; ensure upgrades are cost-neutral for tenants by limiting pass-throughs on rents or linking improvements to long-term savings. Strengthen security of tenure with longer assured periods (3-5 years) and predictable, inflation-linked rent reviews, but maintain flexibility for legitimate landlord needs; create a clear tenancy rights charter and expand deposit protection and independent dispute resolution so repairs are done promptly and tenants feel safe. Local licensing or accreditation for landlords in high-need areas could raise standards and share best practices without destroying supply. In practice, a damp flat in my street would be transformed by such upgrades, making it sustainable for tenants and landlords alike.

I think the key to improving security, affordability and standards for private renters, while keeping a sustainable rental market, is to rebalance protections and support so long‑term tenants aren’t squeezed out by market shifts and by gaps in the welfare system. Two concrete areas stand out for me: bringing holiday lets and second homes back into balance with local housing needs, and reforming Local Housing Allowance (LHA) so it accurately reflects local rents and reduces arrears and homelessness risk. 

Tackling holiday lets and second-home concentrations locally
- Local licensing and sensible caps. Councils should have the power to license short‑term lets and impose caps on concentrations in given neighbourhoods. A practical approach would be to set a transparent cap on the share of housing stock that can operate as holiday lets in a locality, with the ability to adjust based on size and needs. Where licensing is granted, properties would need to meet safety and energy standards, ensuring they are fit for letting and that the local community isn’t adversely affected. Revenue from licensing could fund enforcement, compliance checks, and community services.
- Protect long‑term lets first. The aim is not to punish legitimate tourism but to protect the availability of homes for long‑term residents. In our area, a noticeable cluster of properties used as holiday lets has reduced the number of homes available for families and created pressure on local schools and GP services. A targeted licensing regime would help us keep a stable mix of homes—especially 2‑ to 4‑bedroom family rentals—while preserving vibrant communities.
- Standards and enforcement. Licensing should accompany a clear set of requirements: mandatory safety checks (gas, electrical, fire safety), decent energy efficiency (progressively higher EPC standards), and robust ongoing compliance. Platforms hosting short‑lets should cooperate with local authorities to ensure listings are accurate and compliant.

Reforming Local Housing Allowance to reflect local realities
- Align LHA with local rents and update more frequently. LHA is meant to bridge the gap between what tenants can afford and what the market charges, but in fast‑changing local markets it can lag behind. I’d like to see LHA rates tied to current local rent data, with regular updates (quarterly or bi‑annually) so the benefit keeps pace with market movements.
- Improve affordability and reduce arrears risk. Where LHA does not cover actual rents, tenants struggle to keep up, risking arrears and homelessness. A practical improvement would be automatic or expedited housing‑cost support for tenants whose rents exceed LHA, along with faster processing for Discretionary Housing Payments and easier access to budgeting and debt‑advice services. It would also help landlords if a portion of rent shortfalls could be paid directly to them while a claim is finalised, reducing the cash flow gaps that often lead to evictions.
- Support for landlords to participate. To sustain a healthy private rental sector, landlords need clear, timely guidance on how benefits interact with rents, plus incentives to accept tenants who rely on LHA. Streamlining and simplifying the claimant experience, alongside guaranteed and timely payments, would reduce hesitancy among landlords to rent to benefit recipients.
- Safeguards and tenancy resilience. Alongside LHA reform, ensure longer tenancy stability by supporting longer‑term assured shorthold arrangements where renters want them, with reasonable rent reviews and protections against unfair eviction. Improve deposit protections and access to independent tenancy advice, so renters aren’t incentivised to tolerate poor conditions or insecure housing just to avoid homelessness.

A practical path forward
I would welcome pilots in a few authorities to test a coordinated package: clear local caps on short‑term lets, a streamlined licensing regime with safety and energy standards, and an updated, more responsive LHA framework. Transparent reporting of outcomes—such as changes in long‑term rental stock, numbers of licensed holiday lets, and tenant arrears rates—would help refine the model before wider rollout. The goal should be to deliver more secure, affordable, and better‑quality private rental homes without starving the market of supply or harming legitimate tourism.

In short, combining targeted local controls on holiday lets with smarter, faster housing support would help protect long‑term rentals, reduce homelessness risk, and raise the standard of privately rented homes. That aligns with my broader view that policy should empower local areas to deliver practical, high‑quality housing outcomes for residents while maintaining a viable rental sector.

Introduce clear safety, habitability and energy-efficiency standards with funded retrofit support to cut bills, protect health, and keep rents affordable; ensure sensible enforcement and transition timelines to preserve a sustainable private rental market.

Living in England, in a town outside a big city, and sharing a rented terrace with friends, I’ve seen how private renting can feel insecure and expensive. To improve security, affordability and standards, we need a package that protects tenants without squeezing landlords. 

- Security: make tenancies longer by default (12 months or more) with a clear renewal process; cap unwelcome rent rises to reflect inflation or local norms; strengthen protections against no-fault evictions and make deposit protection compulsory with a fast, independent dispute route; require landlords to complete urgent repairs within strict deadlines and publish response times. 

- Affordability and energy: fund retrofits of older homes through grants and tax incentives for small landlords; raise the minimum energy performance standard to EPC C by 2030 for private lets; ensure energy savings are passed on to tenants through lower bills or more stable costs; remove upfront fees for tenants and cap renewal costs. 

- Standards and sustainability: enforce strict decency and damp-proofing standards, with regular inspections; provide streamlined, low-cost processes for small builders to increase the supply of good-quality, energy-efficient homes locally. 

In my current shared house, damp and slow repairs cost us comfort and money; a fairer system with retrofit grants and longer, secure tenancies would make renting more livable while keeping the market viable.

From my perspective as someone who has lived in England for many years and is now in retirement, I want a private rented sector that feels secure, affordable and well run, but without dampening the supply of homes. The balance is delicate. Here are changes I believe would improve security, affordability and standards for private renters, while keeping the market sustainable in the long term.

- Targeted, sensible rent stability alongside clear uplift rules: I’m in favour of the principle of limits on excessive rent rises, but I’d prefer a targeted approach rather than blanket caps. Local authorities could pilot rent‑stabilisation tied to local cost rents or CPI, with transparent benchmarks and regular reviews. Allow reasonable increases when landlords fund substantial improvements or energy‑efficiency upgrades, and ensure the rules are clear for both new and existing tenancies. The aim is predictable housing costs for renters, not to discourage investment in the sector.
- Longer, secure tenancies with predictable reviews: Encourage longer fixed terms (for example 3–5 years) with formal rent reviews at set points. This would bring some stability for households who rely on a steady home close to services, mobility needs or family, while still giving landlords a clear, lawful path to adjust rents when justified.
- Fast, low‑cost tribunals and funded tenant advice: A properly funded framework of dispute resolution is essential. Renters should have access to free or low‑cost mediation, advice and representation. Fast, efficient tribunals and clear mediation pathways reduce fear of reprisal and help resolve issues such as repairs, deposits, or unfair charges without lengthy, expensive processes.
- Stronger local enforcement and meaningful sanctions: We need robust enforcement of safety and quality standards. That means more frequent inspections where necessary, prompt enforcement actions for hazards, and meaningful penalties for non‑compliant landlords. A public register of enforcement actions and landlord performance could help tenants make informed choices and encourage better practice across the sector.
- Clear protections around safety and energy efficiency: Landlords should meet essential safety standards—gas safety certificates, electrical installation conditions, smoke and CO detectors, and regular energy‑efficiency improvements. Local authorities could require Improvement Notices where needed and support landlords to achieve energy upgrades through grants or affordable loan schemes.
- Fair, transparent fees and deposits: Debates about deposits and fees can add stress to renting. I’d support caps on upfront fees, a standardised, simple deposit protection scheme, and clear, timely return of deposits at the end of a tenancy. This helps older tenants who may have limited cash buffers.
- Support for energy bills and retrofit: Tie improvements in the private sector to wider retrofit ambitions. Offer grants or low‑interest loans for landlords to upgrade insulation, heating systems and energy efficiency, with incentives for newer, well‑managed builds such as Build‑to‑Rent projects that are designed to be long‑term homes with professional management.
- Information, transparency and choice: Require clearer information at the outset about expected rent increases, maintenance standards, and what the tenancy includes (services, community facilities, accessibility features). This transparency helps families and older residents alike to make informed decisions and reduces later disputes.

I’ve seen how a nearby Build‑to‑Rent development with on‑site management keeps rent costs more predictable and repairs quicker. But I’ve also witnessed the instability of some private lets that rise sharply or become difficult to renew after family changes. The changes above aim to preserve the benefits of a flexible market—while giving tenants real protections and landlords a clear framework within which to operate. Crucially, any policy package should be evidence‑led, time‑bound where possible, and accompanied by adequate funding for enforcement, advice services and energy‑efficiency programmes.

If policymakers can deliver a balanced package like this, I believe we can improve security, affordability and standards for private renters, maintain a sustainable rental market, and help older residents stay in communities near the services and support they need.
Agree: reform Local Housing Allowance to reflect local rents to cut arrears and homelessness, and support rent caps or indexation with targeted subsidies to curb spikes without harming supply.

From our experience representing older residents in England, privately rented housing often misses the mark on security, affordability and decent standards, while the market remains essential for many. To improve all three without undermining supply, I would support a package of changes.

- Security of tenure: longer, renewable assured tenancy arrangements with clear, reasonable notice; stronger protection from eviction for vulnerable tenants who fear losing their home.

- Repairs and standards: enforce robust timelines for essential repairs; address damp, mould, heating and ventilation promptly; raise minimum energy efficiency standards and provide funding to landlords to upgrade where costs would otherwise be a barrier.

- Affordability: cap annual rent rises in line with inflation or earnings growth; expand housing benefit for private renters and improve transparency around service charges.

- Incentives and support: grants or tax reliefs to retrofit energy efficiency in private lets; targeted help for older tenants to access safe, affordable homes near essential services.

- Access to suitable downsized homes: more adaptable, well-located private lets designed for older residents, with sensible energy costs.

Taken together, these changes would reduce cold-related health issues and hospital visits, help households budget more reliably, and keep the private rented sector viable for those who need it.

From our experience in a rural town in England, improving security, affordability and standards for private renters must sit alongside delivery of infrastructure and a realistic, locally funded developer contribution. We need longer, more secure tenancies and clearer protections against eviction, with fair, transparent rent reviews and prompt repairs. Tenants should be able to access energy-efficient homes that are affordable to heat; that means higher minimum standards and a clear timetable for upgrades where needed. Affordability will require targeted measures rather than blanket caps—encouraging a mix of private and professionally managed rental stock, with incentives to maintain long-term lettings. New developments should come with transport, schools, GP capacity and utilities; contributions should be planned and phased so services never lag behind housing. To protect the long-term rental pool in communities facing tourist pressure, local licensing or caps on holiday lets and second-home concentrations should be considered. This ensures normal rental supply isn’t siphoned off, while revenues can fund enforcement and local infrastructure. In my area, limited bus links and GP capacity already constrain take-up; better coordination between developers and local authorities would help ensure new private rentals actually serve local households.

From our organisation’s perspective in Scotland, private renters should enjoy stronger protection without compromising a healthy rental market. To improve security, affordability and standards, I support tightening eviction grounds and protections against no-fault and retaliatory evictions, paired with practical rights for tenants. Suggested steps include: extending minimum notice periods for landlord-initiated evictions to six months, with longer notice for rent arrears or problematic behaviour; explicit prohibition of retaliatory eviction when tenants raise repairs or safety concerns; giving tenants a right to appeal eviction decisions to an independent tribunal with timely determinations; and requiring deposits to be securely protected with clear penalties for misuse. Standards must rise too: mandatory, enforceable minimum repairs, annual gas safety and electrical checks, and a clear path to energy efficiency improvements (targeting EPC C within a reasonable timeframe). Affordability could be supported by capping unreasonable rent increases to inflation plus a modest margin and providing incentives for compliant landlords to maintain quality properties. In Glasgow and across Scotland, I’ve seen families face disruption after delays to essential repairs or pressure during disputes; stronger protections would stabilise tenancies and improve living conditions while maintaining a sustainable supply of private rental homes.

Agree that changes should be practical, rights-based and aligned with sustainable communities. In Wales, private renters include many vulnerable groups who too often face discrimination and barriers to adaptations. To boost security, I would back longer assured tenancies with guaranteed renewals and stronger protections agains no-fault and retaliatory evictions: longer notice periods (2–3 months), a right to challenge evictions via an independent review, and a clear just-cause framework for ending tenancies. Landlords would need to show credible grounds, such as non-payment, damage beyond normal wear, or redevelopment plans. For affordability, rents in Build-to-Rent should carry affordability covenants and be CPI-indexed, with rents kept in step with local incomes. Deposits should be protected and affordable, and targeted support offered to disabled and vulnerable renters to cover essential adaptationss and energy costs. Standards must improve: mandatory on-site management for larger schemes, prompt repairs, and upgrades to energy efficiency. Accessibility adaptations—widened doorways, step-free access, hearing/visual supports—should be funded or incentivised. Anti-discrimination enforcement must be strengthened so BAME, disabled, older and younger renters receive equal treatment. From my experience, reliable security and predictable costs stabilise communities and help create sustainable rental markets where families can stay long-term without fear of sudden displacement or unaffordable bills.

From a community-focused organisation representing residents in England, we believe the best route to improve security, affordability and standards for private renters while sustaining the market is a coordinated package of supply-and-quality reforms. Planning reform should prioritise brownfield development and enable sensible densities, with requirements that a portion of new private rental homes come through build-to-rent pipelines or be offered with longer, renewable tenancies to stabilise rents. Incentives such as targeted financing, VAT relief, and clearer guidance for small builders would help unlock delivery without compromising quality or safety. 

Expanding social housing remains essential to relieve market pressure, and private renters should benefit from professionally managed BTR developments with clear tenancy terms, strong energy efficiency standards, robust repairs, and transparent complaint handling. Tenancies should be longer by default with fair rent review mechanisms, and deposits protected in government schemes with straightforward dispersal. Local authorities should have a clear licensing and enforcement role to raise safety and quality across the sector. 

From our experience supporting communities, people feel secure when there is predictable pricing, reliable repairs, and visible governance around energy retrofits and ongoing maintenance.

I think there are important gains to be made, but I worry about pushing reforms too far and shrinking the private rented sector, especially for those of us relying on a pension. From my own street I’ve seen private rented homes that are expensive to heat, with old boilers and drafts, yet rents still rise. Better security could come from longer, clearly defined tenancies and a simple, fair route to satisfactory repairs, with penalties for chronic delays. It would help if deposits were protected and disputes resolved quickly, so tenants aren’t left out of pocket or stranded after a bad move. 

Affordability should go hand in hand with standards: require decent energy efficiency upgrades where we can afford them, but provide grants or low-interest loans to landlords so costs don’t just get passed on in rent. Higher minimum standards must be enforced, and there should be support to find more accessible, well-located rentals near services, so older people aren’t forced to drive long distances. I’m cautious about sweeping caps that could deter investment; a balanced approach is needed.

I believe the changes proposed should strengthen security, affordability and standards for private renters, while keeping a sustainable rental market. In many places, holiday lets and second homes are reducing long‑term stock, pushing rents up and making it harder for families to find secure homes. Local licensing or caps on holiday lets, paired with transparent reporting and sensible thresholds, would help councils protect the core rented stock. Revenue from licensing could fund enforcement and affordable housing projects, and exemptions could apply to genuinely new-build schemes to maintain development momentum.

On safety, habitability and energy efficiency, enforceable standards are essential. Mandatory electrical and gas safety checks, working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, and minimum energy efficiency requirements should be backed by funded retrofit support for landlords. In my experience, where grants or low‑cost loans are available to upgrade insulation, heating and ventilation, tenants enjoy lower bills and better comfort without a spike in rents. Such upgrades should be designed to preserve long‑term tenancies and improve property maintenance.

Together, these measures—local regulation of holiday lets, strong safety and efficiency standards, and government-supported retrofits—can deliver safer, more affordable homes with a stable, investable rental market. I’d welcome pilots and rigorous evaluation to refine delivery and scale up where effective.

i strongly believe from my perspective as a long-standing resident in England, private renters need security, fairness and decent standards, but we must keep a sustainable rental market that doesn’t deter investment or lead to fewer homes. I’m strongly supportive of changes that give tenants fast, affordable access to resolution when things go wrong, while also ensuring landlords can manage their properties effectively and still earn a fair return. In practice, that means three things: quick, low-cost dispute resolution; robust, free or affordable tenant advice and mediation services; and a practical package of safety and tenure reforms that creates stability without punitive impact on landlords who maintain good standards.

First, tribunals and dispute resolution should be accessible and affordable. In recent years I’ve seen disputes drag on because process costs are high and the path to a clear outcome isn’t obvious. The goal should be a streamlined system where tenants can raise repairs, disrepair, or deposit issues with minimal cost and with a binding decision in a reasonable time. Proposals I’d support include a unified online portal for private-rented cases, reduced or capped tribunal fees for tenants, and a fast‑track, low‑cost route for straightforward claims. Importantly, the process should allow for early mediation to resolve issues before a hearing, saving time and stress for both sides. I know families in my community who could have avoided months of anxiety if there had been accessible mediation early on rather than escalating to court.

Second, funded tenant advice services are essential. Independent guidance helps tenants understand their rights, prepare credible evidence, and communicate clearly with landlords. Local authority-funded or locally delivered services, together with Citizens Advice and housing associations, should offer free or low-cost advice, representation where needed for complex disputes, and practical help with things like safety checks and repairs. Concrete examples from the local experience

In my area, affordability and stability rely on these coordinated measures.

Implement compulsory landlord/agent registration, licensing and mandatory training to raise management standards; promote longer, multi-year tenancies with smoother renewals to cut churn and costs; strengthen anti-discrimination, accessibility adaptations, and targeted support for disabled, older and vulnerable renters to keep a fair, sustainable market.

INTRODUCE COMPULSORY LANDLORD/AGENT REGISTRATION AND LICENSING WITH MANDATORY TRAINING TO RAISE MANAGEMENT STANDARDS; PROMOTE LONGER, SECURE TENANCIES WITH EASIER RENEWALS; AND BACK PLANNING REFORM AND INCENTIVES FOR BUILD-TO-RENT, BROWNFIELD DEVELOPMENT AND SOCIAL HOUSING TO BOOST SUPPLY AND AFFORDABILITY, WITH SENSIBLE PRICE CONTROLS.

In Wales, private renters deserve security, affordability and decent standards without undermining the market. A balanced package would combine modest price stability, targeted support, stronger standards and careful supply measures. First, introduce a rent-stability framework: allow annual increases but cap them at CPI plus a small margin (for example CPI + 2%), with regional flex where appropriate, and offer longer tenancies to eligible renters. This would damp volatility without disincentivising landlords. Second, strengthen targeted support: increase housing benefit or local housing allowances and provide deposit protection and tenancy advisory services to those most at risk of hardship. Third, improve rights and standards: require landlords to offer renewals and provide secure tenancy terms (e.g., minimum 3-year terms for tenants with support needs); enforce safety checks, energy-efficiency upgrades, and a straightforward national landlord register with penalties for unsafe homes. Fourth, local action on holiday lets: license or cap whole-home holiday lets in areas with tight supply to protect long-term homes, but keep the regime practical. In my town, I have seen a neighbour have to move when a landlord switched to short-term letting, illustrating how shortages harm families. Taken together, these changes would improve security, affordability and standards while keeping a sustainable private rental market.

absolutely renting in my area has shown me how security can feel fragile for ordinary households. Tenants worry about no-fault evictions, deposits stuck in repair disputes, and fixed-term agreements that end up forcing moves just when bills rise. Changes that could help, while keeping a sustainable private rented market, include: longer, secure tenancies by default (at least 2 years) with a straightforward renewal process and clear, justified eviction grounds; stronger deposit protection and clearer timelines for returning deposits; and tighter controls on letting fees to stop upfront costs that deter families.

Affordability would improve with rent increase limits linked to inflation, longer notice periods, and a national retrofit fund so landlords can upgrade insulation and heating without pushing rents up. Standards must rise too: mandatory timely repairs; regular safety checks for fire and gas; and energy efficiency upgrades supported by grants, moving properties from EPC E toward C on a realistic timetable. Small landlords need practical support (low‑interest loans, simplified compliance) to stay in the market rather than be priced out.

Together, these reforms would boost security and quality without destabilising the sector, and could genuinely cut bills for many renters while keeping a viable private rented market for the longer term!

Thank you for the opportunity to contribute. In Northern Ireland, private renters, including older households, need secure, safe, affordable homes. I support three concrete changes to improve security, affordability and standards while keeping a sustainable market. 

1) Enforceable safety, habitability and energy standards with funded retrofit support. This means mandatory gas safety certificates every year, electrical safety checks every five years, and all rental homes equipped with working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. Tie energy efficiency improvements to tenancy events, with grants or low‑interest loans to upgrade insulation, boilers, and heat pumps. Raise EPC targets toward C or B over time, backed by robust enforcement and clear repair duties so tenants aren’t paying the price of cold, damp homes.

2) Reform Local Housing Allowance to reflect local rents, reducing arrears and homelessness risk. Uprate benefits using local market indices so rents are genuinely covered, with safeguards to prevent sudden or unfair cuts that push households into poverty.

3) Compulsory landlord/agent registration, licensing and training. A simple registration scheme with penalties for non‑compliance, plus accredited training on tenancy management, safety, energy upgrades and tenancy law. Provide accessible funding or transitional routes for small landlords to meet standards without exiting the market.

I’d welcome pilots and strong monitoring to ensure we protect tenants while sustaining supply.

From my experience in a Scottish town, private renters often live with insecurity, damp flats, and energy bills that wipe out any apparent saving. To improve security, affordability and standards while keeping a sustainable rental market, I’d advocate a pragmatic mix of measures: longer tenancy terms with predictable, CPI-linked rent increases to help households plan; robust deposit protection and accessible, quick dispute resolution to reduce fear of eviction over minor arrears. For standards, insist on timely repairs for damp and mould, working smoke and CO detectors, and regular safety checks; give local councils a light-touch landlord licensing scheme funded to support improvements rather than punish landlords. On affordability and sustainability, require higher energy efficiency in all rented homes and provide grants or low-interest loans to landlords for insulation, heat pumps, and draught-proofing; the upgrades should be supported rather than deter investment. Finally, targeted support through housing benefit or local allowances will help low-income renters while maintaining a viable private rental market. This balanced approach aligns with keeping homes decent and affordable without choking supply.

absolutely from my experience in this area, the best way to improve security, affordability and standards for private renters without undermining the market is to ensure new rental development is planned with the wider community in mind. That means coordinating new blocks with transport links, local schools, GP surgeries and utilities, and requiring evidence-backed developer contributions to reflect the impact on infrastructure and services. In practice, this should include clear affordability covenants within private schemes, high energy standards, and professional on-site management that handles repairs promptly. I’m keen on minimum or multi-year tenancies and easier renewal processes, so households aren’t disrupted by churn or moving costs; three-year contracts with straightforward renewals would make budgeting and stability easier for families and older residents alike. For context, a recent build-to-rent block near the station showed how on-site management can keep standards high and repairs swift, and longer tenancies reduced neighbour churn. In exchange for stability, rents should be predictable and linked to local benchmarks, with transparent renewal terms and sensible limits on annual increases. This balanced approach keeps the rental market sustainable while delivering better homes and communities!

Living in England and renting long enough to see the daily realities of the private sector, I want a package of changes that makes security, affordability and standards genuinely meaningful—without killing off the private market or pushing people into worse housing altogether. I’ll keep my views aligned with the practical approach I’ve outlined before: retain a healthy, well-managed private sector while strengthening protections for renters, especially those who are vulnerable.

Security and anti‑discrimination, with better access to adaptations, are foundational. People shouldn’t have to choose between a safe home and reasonable access. I support stronger enforcement against discrimination in letting and tenancy decisions, and I’d like to see clearer duties on landlords to make reasonable adaptations for disabled tenants without fear of losing the home. That could be funded through targeted grants or tax relief for adaptations, plus a streamlined route for tenants to request changes (with timely responses and clear responsibilities for landlords). We also need proactive support for older or disabled tenants who may need longer-term arrangements or practical help to stay in a neighbourhood they know and can afford.

Accessibility in practice must go beyond compliance. It means wider doorways, step-free entries, lifts where appropriate, visual and hearing aids for safety alarms, and flexible layouts that can adapt to changing needs. When landlords and letting agents understand and plan for these needs as a standard part of property management, tenants are less likely to face relocation as circumstances change. A good example is a block I know where bids for accessible retrofit were rushed and poorly managed; tenants with mobility needs couldn’t use parts of the building, and repairs dragged on. If there were a guaranteed route to fund essential adaptations and a mandatory minimum standard for accessibility in new lets, we’d all benefit.

Tenancy security should be a default, not an afterthought. The private sector should offer longer, renewable tenancies by default with predictable and fair rent progression. That might include a baseline 12‑month tenancy with a cap on year‑on‑year rent increases (for example CPI plus a small, capped margin or a fixed cap), plus robust protections against retaliatory evictions. Deposits and dispute resolution must be fair and transparent, with independent mediation available early to head off costly court cases. A key element is portability: if a tenant moves within a landlord group or between properties in the same management scheme, their tenancy should transfer smoothly, with their accrued rights preserved.

Affordability has to be addressed without dampening supply. On top of cap‑and‑stability measures, targeted subsidies should accompany rent oversight to prevent distortions in the market. Rents shouldn’t outpace earnings or living costs, particularly for families and workers just starting out. In addition to caps, I’d advocate for targeted housing benefits and a more transparent mechanism for rent refunds or discounts when a property fails to meet agreed maintenance standards. Energy costs are a big part of affordability; properties should be required to meet energy‑efficiency benchmarks (e.g., EPC band C or better by 2030 where feasible) and landlords should be supported to retrofit where gaps exist. I’ve seen bills spike in winter because of poor insulation, and even a small upgrade could save households hundreds of pounds a year.

Standards and professional management matter, especially in a market with a lot of variation in quality. Strengthened minimum standards for safety and maintenance—smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, annual gas checks, accessible emergency responses, and timely repairs—should be mandatory, with enforcement and random inspections. Landlords should be encouraged to join accredited management schemes that require service standards, tenant engagement, and clear channels for feedback. In practice, good management makes a real difference: a block I know has a dedicated property manager, rapid response times, and regular resident meetings, and that makes a big difference to neighbours and overall community morale.

Supply remains essential for long‑term affordability. Planning reform should simplify and speed up consent for brownfield development and incentivise build‑to‑rent that includes genuine affordability and long‑term stewardship. The case for social housing expansion and green/light‑touch incentives for SME builders is clear: a diversified stock that includes social, affordable private, and market homes helps stabilise rents and reduce pressure on the most vulnerable.

In my area, the contrast is telling. Some newer BTR schemes with on‑site managers feel well‑run and provide stable rents and good maintenance; others fall short on repairs or lack accessible designs, leaving tenants to navigate a maze of agencies. If reforms deliver stronger protections, predictable rents, better accessibility, and smarter planning that increases supply without lowering standards, I think the private rented sector can contribute positively to local communities while remaining affordable and sustainable for households like mine.

Overall, I’d support a balanced package: strengthen protections and accessibility, introduce sensible rent‑growth controls with targeted subsidies, and push for planning reforms that unlock well‑designed, accessible, affordable supply—especially on brownfield sites and through build‑to‑rent with long‑term stewardship. That combination offers security for renters, value for money, and a healthier, more sustainable market for years to come.

To improve security, affordability and standards for private renters while keeping the market sustainable, we need a package that boosts supply and raises protections without stifling investment. First, plan for growth: reform planning rules to accelerate brownfield development and incentivise build‑to‑rent and social housing expansion. Require a share of new PRS on major sites to be affordable or professionally managed, with clear, faster planning routes, viability support up front, and predictable infrastructure timelines. In our area, planning delays on viable brownfield sites often derail schemes that could have delivered decent homes with better management.

Second, tighten safety and energy standards with practical funding to retrofit. Enforceable safety, habitability and energy-efficiency targets should sit alongside funded retrofit support so landlords can upgrade heating, insulation and ventilation without passing crippling costs to tenants. A national retrofit fund or accessible, low‑interest loan mechanism would help keep bills down and health up.

Third, raise professional standards via compulsory landlord and agent registration, licensing and mandatory training. A simple, affordable registration system funded by fees would improve compliance, enable consistent enforcement and signal to tenants that renting is a professional service. With enforcement and retrofit funding in place, these reforms can lift standards while keeping a sustainable, attractive rental sector.

Advocate a balanced approach: strengthen security of tenure and energy efficiency in private lets, while using targeted subsidies or indexation-linked relief to curb rent rises Obviously.... Be wary that broad caps could suppress new rental supply and harm sustainability.

I believe the most effective changes to private rental are those that strengthen security for tenants while keeping a sustainable market. No-fault and retaliatory evictions undermine affordability and stability, so we should harden protections around them. In my experience locally, when tenants raise repairs, threats of eviction quickly follow, and that fear makes people stay in unsuitable homes. We need clearer eviction grounds, with transparent, evidence-based reasons and longer notice. For periodic tenancies, a minimum six-month notice for eviction with a valid cause; for terminations, a straightforward process tied to the contract end date. Importantly, there should be no eviction while serious repairs or safety investigations are underway.

Add robust appeal rights: tenants should be able to challenge eviction decisions before an independent housing tribunal, with suspensive relief available during the review. Couple this with stronger minimum standards—prompt repairs, safe heating, basic energy efficiency—and deposit protections to prevent who pays the price when a landlord runs into trouble. Consider a cap or justified basis for rent increases, aligned to market data, to preserve affordability.

These protections would reduce insecurity, support families staying in stable homes, and still allow landlords to operate viably. They align with my view that reforms should target real barriers to secure, decent housing without tipping the balance away from responsible landlords or the wider rental market.

I support compulsory landlord/agent registration, licensing and mandatory training; it would raise management and safety standards, curb rogue practices, and complement targeted funding to sustain a fair, secure private rental market.

To improve security, affordability and standards for private renters while keeping a sustainable rental market, I favour a careful mix of protections and targeted support alongside the planning reforms I’ve already supported to boost supply. First, a rent-stabilisation or cap system that limits annual increases to CPI (with a sensible cap) and applies to most standard lets, but allows longer tenancies and genuine cost passthrough for major works. This would help households on fixed incomes feel more secure when renewing, rather than facing endless squeeze every year. Second, encourage longer fixed-term leases (2-3 years) with predictable, modest increases, so families can stay put without fear of rapid rent hikes at every renewal. Third, stronger enforcement of standards: enforceable minimum energy efficiency (targeting EPC B over time), mandatory annual safety checks, and penalties for rogue landlords. Fourth, targeted subsidies and local housing allowances to bridge gaps in high-demand areas, plus incentives for landlords to upgrade energy efficiency and maintain good-quality homes. Fifth, mandatorily publish transparent local rent data to help renters compare and plan. Finally, ensure planning reforms continue to expand supply so increases in rents aren’t solely supply-driven, while protecting green space and environmental safeguards. In our borough, clearer rules and practical support would help many households without deterring responsible investment.

AS AN ORGANISATION, WE BELIEVE THE PRIVATE RENTED SECTOR CAN BE SECURE, AFFORDABLE AND WELL GOVERNED WITHOUT DRIVING UP RENTAL COSTS OR REDUCING SUPPLY. THE CHANGES BELOW WOULD STRIKE THAT BALANCE BY PROTECTING SMALL LANDLORDS WHILE ROOTING OUT THE MOST HARMFUL SPECULATIVE BEHAVIOUR AND DELIVERING SAFER HOMES.

- TAX, MORTGAGE AND INCENTIVES TO PROTECT SMALL LANDLORDS AND DETER SPECULATIVE EXITS: INTRODUCE TARGETED RELIEF FOR SMALL PORTFOLIO LANDLORDS WHO OFFER STABLE, LONG‑TERM TENANCIES, WHILE CLOSING PERVERSE INCENTIVES THAT FAVOUR RAPID TURNOVER. CONSIDER MORTGAGE SUPPORT OR TAX CREDITS FOR LANDLORDS WHO REFURBISH AND MAINTAIN PROPERTIES, PAIRED WITH STRONGER SIGNALS THAT LARGE-SCALE BUY-TO-LET ACTIVITY WILL BE TAXED OR LIMITED. THIS KEEPS VIABLE LETTINGS IN THE MARKET AND DISCOURAGES SUDDEN EXITS THAT DESTABILISE SUPPLY.

- ENFORCEABLE SAFETY, HABITABILITY AND ENERGY STANDARDS WITH FUNDED RETROFIT: REQUIRE REGULAR SAFETY CHECKS (GAS, ELECTRICAL) AND ENSURE PROPERTIES MEET MINIMUM ENERGY EFFICIENCY (TARGET EPC C WHERE FEASIBLE) WITH FUNDED RETROFIT SUPPORT. GRANTS OR LOW-COST LOANS SHOULD COVER UPGRADE COSTS, WITH PROTECTIONS SO TENANTS BENEFIT FROM LOWER BILLS AND HEALTHIER LIVING CONDITIONS.

- STRONGER LOCAL ENFORCEMENT AND MEANINGFUL SANCTIONS: EMPOWER COUNCILS WITH ROBUST INSPECTION POWERS, TIMELY IMPROVEMENT NOTICES AND REALISTIC PENALTIES FOR NON-COMPLIANCE. A TARGETED LICENSING FRAMEWORK COULD ENSURE ACCOUNTABILITY, BACKED BY DEDICATED ENFORCEMENT FUNDING SO STANDARDS AND TENANT RIGHTS ARE RELIABLY UPHELD.

THESE CHANGES WOULD SUSTAIN A HEALTHY PRIVATE RENTED MARKET WHILE DELIVERING SAFER, MORE AFFORDABLE HOMES FOR TENANTS.

To improve security, affordability and standards for private renters while keeping a sustainable rental market, three changes would help. First, empower local authorities with stronger enforcement and meaningful sanctions. This means mandatory, regular inspections of private rented homes for fire, gas, electrical safety, damp and heating issues, with clear deadlines and penalties for non-compliance. Expanding licensing—such as selective or additional licensing for higher-risk streets or areas—and publishing landlords’ performance would deter negligence and protect tenants’ rights. In our village, tenants have reported safety and maintenance delays; a robust local framework would address these problems quickly and transparently. Second, curb holiday lets and second-home pressures through local licensing or caps, tied to occupancy and community impact. This would safeguard long-term rental stock for local families and help stabilise rents. Third, design targeted tax, mortgage and incentive measures that protect small landlords while discouraging speculative exit. Think targeted tax relief for genuinely rented homes, grants or low-interest financing for essential safety and energy upgrades, and sensible limits on large-scale buy-to-let exits, with support for landlords who commit to long-term tenancies. Taken together, these steps would raise standards, improve security and keep rents affordable without wrecking a sustainable market.

From my experience in Scotland’s rural communities, the private rented sector works best when tenants feel secure, affordable, and treated fairly. To improve security, affordability and standards while keeping a sustainable market, I support:
- Strengthening grounds, notice periods and appeal rights to curb no-fault evictions and retaliatory actions. Longer, predictable notice and accessible routes to challenge unfair moves would give households time to plan and rely less on temporary arrangements.
- Compulsory landlord/agent registration, licensing, and mandatory training or accreditation. A straightforward registration scheme would ensure properties meet basic safety and energy-efficiency standards, require up-to-date gas and electrical checks, and promote good practice in repairs and tenant communication. Licensing could fund local enforcement and support for landlords to meet standards rather than creating unnecessary red tape.
- Strong anti-discrimination protections, plus accessibility adaptations and tailored support for disabled, BAME, older, young and other vulnerable renters. More accessible homes, clear information, and targeted advice when repairs or rent increases are due will help households stay in their communities.
In practice, these measures would stabilise rents, reduce turnover, and encourage responsible investment in energy efficiency—helping to build a higher-quality, affordable private rented sector across rural Scotland while protecting landscapes and local services.

Encourage small landlords with targeted tax relief and mortgage incentives to stay in the market, while deterring speculative exits; set enforceable safety, habitability and energy-efficiency standards, backed by funded retrofit support to cut bills and protect tenants.

I rent privately in England and want a rental sector that is affordable, safe and liveable, while still viable for landlords and letting agents. Two changes would make the biggest difference.

First, reform Local Housing Allowance and housing benefit interactions so they reflect local rents. Too often LHA rates lag the actual rents in my area, driving arrears and increasing homelessness risk when payments are late or insufficient. I know tenants who struggle after delays in benefits, or when a landlord refuses to renew a tenancy because the payments won't cover the new rent. Align rates with local market, with annual reviews and quick processing, plus a contingency for council tax or utilities. This would keep households in accommodation and reduce distress.

Second, set enforceable safety, habitability and energy efficiency standards with funded retrofit support. A damp flat with poor insulation costs more in winter and harms health. If landlords are required to meet safety checks, maintain reasonable living conditions, and upgrade insulation and efficient heating through government retrofit funding, bills fall and health improves. This must be supported by grants or low-cost loans to cover upfront costs.

Together, these changes would stabilise costs, improve living conditions and sustain a fair, green private rental market.

From where I stand, in England and at my age, the goal of improving security, affordability and standards for private renters must be paired with sensible checks on development and a properly supported system for tenants to access help and resolution. We can’t have more red tape everywhere, but we also can’t accept a market that leaves vulnerable tenants in damp, unsafe homes while developers rush schemes through. The balance I’d want to see rests on targeted enforcement, accountable planning contributions, better council capacity, and strong but practical tenant support.

What this should mean in practice:

- Smarter enforcement with real consequences for non-delivery: continue to tighten licencing where there are genuine hotspots of poor quality or rogue operators, but fund local authorities so compliant landlords aren’t caught in unnecessary cost and bureaucracy. Pair licensing with a clear pathway to uplift properties—grants or low‑interest loans for insulation, damp, heating and energy efficiency—and a straightforward compliance route so good landlords aren’t penalised. Create a robust, publicly accessible delivery tracker for affordable housing obligations tied to planning conditions, with clearly defined penalties for late or non-delivery and transparent consequences for developers who repeatedly miss targets. This isn’t punitive for the many; it’s accountability for the few who undermine the market.

- Ensure new rental development is coordinated with infrastructure: new homes should be expected to sit alongside robust transport links, schools, healthcare facilities and reliable utilities. Developer contributions must be realistic and timely, backed by enforceable timetables and penalties if delivery slips. In practice, I’ve seen promising schemes falter because infrastructure plans lag behind housing. We should demand clear, trackable contributions—via planning obligations that are not just promises on paper, but safeguarded and delivered, with independent monitoring and public reporting.

- Stronger planning and sector accountability: councils need the resources to plan, monitor and enforce planning conditions. Too often affordable housing promises tied to major developments fail to materialise or arrive late. We should fund planning and enforcement teams adequately, require regular reporting on Section 106 and similar obligations, and ensure there are real consequences for repeated under-delivery. A transparent pipeline helps: tenants and communities can see when and where affordable homes are due and hold developers to account.

- Tenant support that reduces fear and speeds resolution: fast, low-cost tribunals and mediation services are essential, along with funded tenant advice centers that are easy to access and independent. The fear of reprisals must not silence tenants who raise problems. I’ve witnessed neighbours hesitate to report damp or unsafe conditions because even simple steps take months. A dedicated advisory service, combined with quick, affordable dispute resolution, would cut through delays and get decent homes back on track. Tenancies should offer stability, with a default term long enough to provide security (two to three years with renewal options) but with fair provisions for maintenance, reasonable rent reviews, and straightforward pathways for landlords to regain possession for legitimate reasons with proper notice and compensation for modernisation costs.

- Maintenance, repairs and energy standards: high standard, well‑maintained homes should be the baseline. Landlords must be obliged to carry out repairs promptly and to meet minimum energy efficiency standards, with support available to fund improvements. Where landlords fall short, penalties should be swift and proportionate, but the routes to compliance should be accessible so that well‑meaning landlords aren’t squeezed out of the market by disproportionate costs.

- Protect a sustainable market: the aim isn’t to punish private landlords but to ensure the market delivers safe, affordable homes and public benefit. We should protect the supply of private rentals by avoiding overly broad licensing regimes that deter compliant landlords, while keeping strong enforcement against the worst actors. Targeted action, transparent reporting, and real consequences for failing to deliver will help maintain supply while lifting standards.

In short, a package that combines targeted enforcement and effective planning with well-resourced tenant support and practical infrastructure commitments will move us toward more secure, affordable and higher‑quality private rentals without choking the market. I’ve seen the gaps in my area—delays in infrastructure, patchy enforcement, and a slow path to resolution for tenants. If we fix those levers, we’ll deliver real improvements where they matter most for families and older people alike.

Living in England and trying to balance a reasonable renting situation near work and family, I think we need changes that make private renting more secure, affordable and better regulated, but without wrecking the market that currently supplies a lot of homes. If reforms are well targeted and adequately funded, they can improve security and affordability for privatr renters while expanding quality supply and avoiding unintended consequences for the wider market. With clear milestones, transparency and properr funding for planning and enforcement, we can move private renting toward greater security and affordability while keeping a sustainablr rental market for the years ahead.

As someone who sees how our local housing market shifts when holiday lets and second homes proliferate, I think the best way to improve security, affordability and standards is a measured mix of targeted restrictions and higher professional standards, tested through pilots rather than blanket rules.

First, local licensing or caps on holiday lets and second homes in areas with real long-term rental pressure would help protect the stock families rely on. In my area, properties switch to short‑term letting in peak season, squeezing long‑term rents and changing communities. A controlled licensing regime would help councils monitor and respond quickly.

Second, compulsory landlord/agent registration, licensing and mandatory training would raise day‑to‑day management and safety standards. A simple accreditation for safety checks, energy efficiency, and tenant rights would reduce poor practice. Importantly, keep exemptions for genuinely small-scale landlords and offer streamlined digital processes to avoid red tape.

Enforcement and data are crucial: real‑time publication of licensed properties, penalties for non‑compliance, and funding for local teams to process registrations. Run this as a 12–24 month pilot in high‑concentration areas, review results before scaling up.

Overall, these steps should stabilise long-term supply, raise quality and protect communities without choking legitimate investment.

In England, I want a private rented sector that is secure, affordable and well managed, but still supports a sustainable market for new homes. Three linked changes would achieve this. First, compulsory landlord and agent registration, licensing and mandatory training or accreditation for property managers. This would lift basic standards, ensure timely repairs and clear tenancy protections, and reduce rogue operators. Our Build‑to‑Rent pilots show that professional management and clear compliance expectations translate into fewer complaints and better energy‑efficiency retrofits. Second, boost affordable supply through planning reform and incentives for Build‑to‑Rent, brownfield development and social housing expansion. Streamlined approvals and affordable covenants on new stock can rapidly grow good quality homes without adding pressure on greenfield sites. Third, ensure new rental developments are coordinated with transport, schools, healthcare and utilities, with realistic developer contributions. Tied to independent monitoring and robust evaluation, this approach prevents infrastructure gaps and sustains communities, while protecting tenants. We should anchor these measures in pilots with sunset clauses and rigorous evaluation before scaling, as we did with area‑level pilots to refine policy responsibly.

As an older resident in England, I want private renting to be fair, secure and well maintained, not a guesswork lottery. Too many tenants encounter discrimination, delays getting essential accessibility adaptations, and a sense that tenancies can be ended or rents rise without proper protection. To improve security, affordability and standards while keeping a sustainable market, I would prioritise three strands.

First, stronger rights and support: stricter enforcement against discrimination by letting agents and landlords; mandatory reasonable adjustments for disabled tenants; targeted help for older and vulnerable renters to navigate deposits, repairs and tenancy concerns. Require ongoing energy efficiency and accessible design improvements in new lets.

Second, expand affordable supply through planning reform: incentives for build-to-rent with affordable quotas, faster approvals for brownfield sites, and expanded social housing using public land. Commit upfront funds for infrastructure so schools and GP services aren't overwhelmed.

Third, better control of holiday lets: local licensing or caps to protect long-term stock, plus measures to prevent tourist concentrations from eroding communities.

Example from my town shows the problem: too many holiday lets, and a neighbour waited years for a ramp upgrade that never came. We need enforceable commitments and upfront funding.

From my experience as a tenant and small landlord in England, we need a package that steadies rents without choking supply. I’d support targeted rent caps or stabilisation schemes paired with indexation that reflects local affordability and includes a clear safety valve to avoid unnecessary landlord exits. These should sit alongside targeted subsidies for households most in need, funded through sensible measures like planning gains or local authority schemes, and properly time‑limited so they don’t become permanent distortions. 

Crucially, we must unlock supply: in our borough there are unused public sites that could deliver 60–100 affordable homes if planning uplift is captured and reinvested in infrastructure. Longer tenancy periods (2–3 years) with renewal rights, backed by decent enforcement of safety and energy‑efficiency standards, would raise security and reduce turnover. Strengthen licensing and inspections, but offer practical support to landlords, including advice and improvement loans. If we combine careful rent controls and targeted subsidies with a credible path to more affordable homes, the private rental market can stay sustainable for landlords and secure for tenants.

Across Wales, many private renters worr about security and the costs of moving. To improve security, affordability and standards while keeping a sustainable market, I’d back a pragmatic mix of longer tenancy terms, stronger management standards, and targeted support. First, promote minimum multi-year tenancies (2–3 years) with easier renewals and clear, timely renewal notices, so households can plan and build community ties without constant upheaval. Pair this with predictable, transparent rent review processes and safeguards to prevent sudden increases. Second, make landlord and agent registration compulsory, with mandatory training and a public accreditation scheme. A robust national register and routine inspections would raise maintenance and safety standards and help tenants identify reputabl landlords. Third, strengthen anti-discrimination protections and ensure homes are adaptable. Require accessible design where feasible, plus funding or affordable loans for disability-related adaptations; provide tailored support for disabled, older and vulnerable renters, including BAME and younger households, so they can access appropriate housing. Finally, align standards with energy efficiency and damp prevention, and offer grants or low-interest loans to small landlords for upgrades. Ensure enforcement and tenant guidancee improve, with accessible tenancy advic and straightforward redress channels. Taken together, these steps should stabilise homes, improve quality and preserve a viable private rental sector in Wales.

Introduce enforceable safety, habitability and energy efficiency standards with funded retrofit support to cut bills and protect tenants’ health. Strengthen local enforcement with inspections and meaningful sanctions to ensure standards and tenant rights are upheld, while safeguarding small landlords’ viability to keep a sustainable market.

Reform Local Housing Allowance to reflect local rents to cut arrears and homelessness, and introduce local licensing/caps on holiday lets and second homes to safeguard long-term rental supply; backed by stronger council monitoring and funding.

To improve security, affordability and standards for private renters while keeping a sustainable market, I’d back measures that strengthen eviction protections, extend notice periods, and guard against retaliatory actions, alongside robust safety and energy standards. In practice, this means reforming eviction rules so no-fault evictions are removed or tightly restricted, with landlords required to demonstrate defined grounds and proper notice. For periodic tenancies, a minimum six months’ notice would provide real security; twelve months in cases where tenants have long-standing ties or are vulnerable. Tenants must not be evicted for raising disrepair or safety concerns: retaliatory evictions should be illegal, with swift penalties and an accessible appeals route.

There should also be a formal right to challenge eviction decisions in court, with independent reviews to prevent improper removals. On standards, mandatory safety checks (gas and electrical) and prompt remedies for damp and mould are essential, together with stronger energy-efficiency requirements and accessible grants to help landlords upgrade. Tenancy deposits should be protected and kept affordable, with longer-term contracts enabling affordable rent covenants linked to local incomes.

From conversations in my community, stories of long-term tenants losing their home after raising a problem show why these protections are needed for security and a sustainable private-rented sector.

Fast, low-cost tribunals and funded tenant advice with accessible mediation would resolve issues without fear of reprisals; plus stronger local enforcement, wider inspection powers and meaningful sanctions are essential to raise standards and protect tenant rights, while keeping a sustainable rental market.

From my experience in England as an older resident, private renters need protections that are fast, affordable and enforceable, while the market remains viable for landlords and tenants alike. To achieve this, I would prioritise:
